3	######## PDF 363 (printed 352) ########
4	SUPERTRAINING
5	6.8.3 The Structure of Special Physical Preparedness
6	The above-mentioned characteristics of functional specialisation in multi-year training are associated with 
7	specific adaptive changes in the cardiovascular-respiratory and neuromuscular systems, as well as in the 
8	efficiency of the central nervous mechanisms that regulate their activities. For many years, it was not appreciated 
9	that each type of sport requires not only a distinct type of motor skill, but also a different type of physiological 
10	fitness. Even today, the role and nature of supplementary training is not clearly understood. For example, much 
11	the same sort of resistance training may be prescribed for many different athletes in various sports, simply 
12	because the sports seem to be superficially similar. 
13	It must be realised that supplementary or 'cross' training 
14	cannot simply be used in a very general way in the belief that strength, speed or endurance acquired in one 
15	situation will be of direct benefit to performance in another situation.
16	For example, muscle endurance gained through supplementary running training does not mean that it will 
17	directly improve the performance of a competitive rower or cyclist. Special physical preparedness (SPP) depends 
18	on developing the necessary physiological qualities with the same muscles and neuromuscular mechanisms that 
19	are encountered in the given sport. Therefore, training for special physical preparedness must be based on a 
20	thorough understanding of the different types of specificity discussed in 1.3 and the characteristics of the 
21	interaction between the various organs and the neuromuscular system, which determines the change in special 
22	work capacity.
23	It was also assumed that one could develop each fitness quality separately with some or other form of general 
24	training, then assemble all of them to produce the necessary sport specific fitness from them. The emergence of 
25	specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities, however, is not supported by current physiological and 
26	biochemical research, so it is clear that the management of training must take into consideration the effects of 
27	concurrent and sequential training means. Therefore, the problem of programming training was examined from 
28	several different positions in earlier chapters (see especially 3.2.1 regarding speed and quickness, and 4.4 
29	regarding general endurance).
30	6.9 Preparedness and the Training Load
31	The connection between the athlete's fitness state and a given loading regime is the central issue in the theory and 
32	practice of programming training (sec 6.3). It is also the weakest link in the management of training, which 
33	requires the special attention of scientists and coaches. Before examining the practical aspects of the connection 
34	between loading and the athlete's fitness state, the concepts of training load and training effect must be defined 
35	more thoroughly (see Fig 6.12).
36	Strictly speaking, the training load does not exist as an independent entity. Terminologically, it must be 
37	distinguished from the load used in weight training, which refers to the resistance or force imposed on the body 
38	by a weight or machinc. Training load is related to the muscular work which the body must produce to carry out 
39	a given regime of exercise in training or competition. More precisely, muscular work is that training potential 
40	which elicits an appropriate training effect from the body. Thus, the training potential of muscular work, and 
41	consequently its training effect is to a large extent determined by the athlete’s current fitness state.
42	It should be clear that the interrelation between the athlete's fitness state and the training load is extremely 
43	complex, dependent upon many factors and determined by numerous variables (see Fig 6.12). Unfortunately, 
44	research concerning this connection is limited and often contradictory. 
45	Therefore, this chapter attempts to 
46	systematise and examine the connection between the athlete's fitness state and the training load, drawing largely 
47	upon the results of extensive research by Verkhoshansky and his co-workers.
48	6.9.1 The Training Load and its Effect
49	The training load refers to the quantitative calculation of the training work performed. It is customary to 
50	recognise the concepts of external, internal and psychological loading, i.e. the quantity of work done, its effect on 
51	the body and the psychologically perceived effect on the athlete, respectively (Matveyev, 1964; Volkov, 1969; 
52	Ozolin, 1970; Tumanyan, 1974). Volume and intensity are used as the most general characteristics of the training 
53	load, as defined in 6.2.2 (Ozolin, 1949; Matveyev, 1956; Khomenkov, 1970; Nabatnikova, 1972).
54	There are other classifications of the training load based on the motor characteristics of the sport, the power 
55	of muscular work^ the pedagogical tasks of the training, the effect on restoration, the effect on subsequent work, 
56	the interaction of work regimes of different emphasis (e.g. the interaction of primarily strength work and speed-
57	352
58	
59	
60	######## PDF 364 (printed 353) ########
61	SUPERTRAINING
62	strength work) and other criteria (Farfel, 1958; Volkov, 1969, 1974; Zimkin, 1963; Monogarov & Platonov, 
63	1975; Suslov, 1978; Scherrer, 1962, 1969).
64	However, each of these classifications, applied separately, are not quite suitable for resolving the task of the 
65	programming of training. A somewhat different approach is required here, which provides special requirements 
66	for the preliminary assessment of the loading and takes into account the above classification criteria.
67	The concept of loading suggests firstly a physiological measure of the effect of specialised muscular work on 
68	the body, reflected in the form of specific functional reactions. Consequently the necessity arose, in developing 
69	the concepts of external and internal loading, for introducing the concepts of the training potential of the loading 
70	and its training effect to enable one to more precisely describe the relationship between cause and effect (see 6.3, 
71	especially Fig 6.12).
72	The influence of the loading is expressed by its training effect (TE), assessed, first of all, by the magnitude of 
73	the change in the athlete's fitness state. 
74	Research concerning the forms in which the TE occurs is very 
75	contradictory, generally amounting to the following representation of events in the training process (Zatsiorsky, 
76	1964; Volkov, 1966; Matveyev, 1977):
77	Acute TE > Delayed TE > Cumulative TE.
78	The first two forms are associated with the single training session: the acute TE is the body’s current reaction to 
79	the physical loading, while the delayed TE is the alteration in the athlete's state observed some time after the 
80	workout. The cumulative TE is the result of the subsequent accumulation of all the TEs that were elicited during 
81	training.
82	However, the above scheme is one-sided and does not take into account the qualitative changes in the TE 
83	when they are produced by training loads of different primary emphasis (e.g. on strength, speed-strength or 
84	muscle endurance). The fact is that the accumulation of training effects is not simply a summation of separate 
85	effects, but a synergistic whole (i.e. the sum of the parts is greater than the whole).
86	The mechanism of generalised adaptation as a universal quality of a biological system establishing a balance 
87	between its state and external conditions, is determined primarily by the automatic selection of an accommodative 
88	strategy which is most appropriate in that situation. This involves selective response to the training influences of 
89	different primary emphasis and their stable integration into a well-adapted system. 
90	As has already been 
91	mentioned, the cumulative TE itself can have a different quantitative and qualitative expression, depending on 
92	factors including the current state of fitness, the order in which training regimes of different emphasis follow each 
93	other, the after-effects of preceding loading, and the duration of given training means (Verkhoshansky, 1970).
94	For example, it has long been known that the result of a workout depends on the sequence of exercises (e.g. 
95	with primary emphasis on speed, strength or endurance). Considerable research has shown clearly the effect of a 
96	particular sequence of training loads of different emphasis during long-term training on the body, e.g. 'aerobic' 
97	and 'anaerobic' glycolytic loading for developing special endurance (Nabatnikova, 1972; Volkov, 1975; Platonov, 
98	1980) or strength and jumping exercises for explosive strength (Tatyan, 1975; Khodykin, 1976; Chemousov, 
99	1978; Levchenko, 1980).
100	Based on similar research, it has been suggested that a distinction be made between the concepts of partial 
101	TE (the result of the effect of loading of one primary emphasis or means) and cumulative TE (the result of the 
102	generalised effect on the body of loading of different primary emphasis, applied concurrently or sequentially). In 
103	the latter case there are both quantitative and qualitative aspects to the TE. The distinction between these 
104	concepts can best be explained by examples.
105	In one experiment (Fig 6.24), group 1 began by using barbell exercises, followed by depth-jumps (a 
106	plyometric method of developing explosive strength). Group 2 used the reverse sequence of means. Each group 
107	of means were used for three months each. Group 3 used the barbell exercises and the depth-jumps concurrently 
108	throughout both 3-month stages. The overall volume of the loading was equivalent in all groups.
109	The results of the studies enabled us first of all to compare the partial TE of utilising only barbell exercises 
110	and depth-jumps (the first stage for groups 1 and 2), as well as the cumulative TE obtained as a result o f two 
111	different ways of organising the loading: concurrent (group 3) and sequential (the second stage of groups 1 and 
112	2). The following conclusions were derived from this experiment:
113	1. The partial TE of the depth-jumping is greater than that of the barbell exercises.
114	353
115	
116	
117	######## PDF 365 (printed 354) ########
118	SUPERTRAINING
119	2. The final effect of the training is altered substantially by re-arrangement of the loading of different primary 
120	emphasis. The sequence of using barbell exercises followed by depth-jumps (group 1) produced a higher 
121	level of speed-strength preparedness (a positive cumulative TE), than the reverse sequence (group 2). Id 
122	group 2 the TE was essentially lower at the end of the second stage than after the first (a negative 
123	cumulative TE).
124	3. The concurrent use of the above means in the first stage (group 3) yielded a larger cumulative effect than in 
125	groups 1 and 2. However, the TE noticeably decreased for group 3 during the second stage because the 
126	lengthy use of a single means decreases the training potential of the loading.
127	Figure 6.24 The training effect of different sequences of speed-strength means for high junipers of medium qualification. Graph I 
128	shows the increase in absolute strength of the plantarflexors; graph 2, the increase in maximal explosive effort in a vertical jump; graph 
129	3, the increase in height after a depth jump. All values in % increase over initial values. White bars = first 3 months; shaded bars = next 
130	3 months of training. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
131	In another experiment (Fig 6.25), over a 7-week period, group 1 used weights exercises with 30-50% of IRM; 
132	group 2 used 70-90% of IRM and group 3 used weights of 30-90% of IRM concurrently (i.e. using the 30-50% 
133	and 70-90% regimes together). The general loading in all groups was equivalent in terms of the metabolic cost 
134	of the work. Again it is easy to see the partial TE of using different weights (groups 1 and 2) and the cumulative 
135	TE from the concurrent use of those and other forms of resisted forms of loading (group 3).
136	One should pay special attention to how the cumulative phenomenon appears as a result of combination work 
137	with weights of 30-90% of IRM regarding the power achieved in group 3, and how much higher it is relative to 
138	the partial TE obtained with means of single emphasis (groups 1 and 2). At the same time it should be noted that 
139	the greatest increase in speed was produced by training with loads of 30-50% o f 1 RM (Group 1, graph 2).
140	The data shows clearly how much the athlete's special preparedness depends on the organisation of training 
141	loads, what must be emphasized when organising training, what type of TE is required in each case and what one 
142	needs to do to achieve it.
143	Figure 6.25 The training effect (in % increase) of different loading schemes on highly qualified jumpers for the extensor musclcs of 
144	both legs (Nedobyvailov). Details are given in the text. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
145	From a practical standpoint, it is expedient to assess the TE with respect to two criteria: the temporal (acute and 
146	delayed) and the qualitative (partial and cumulative). The acute TE is the effect observed immediately during or 
147	directly after a training session, while the delayed TE appears a relatively short time after the loading, for 
148	example, in a number of mixed sessions or over a short period (the short-term TE), or preserved for a longer time
149	354
150	
151	
152	######## PDF 366 (printed 355) ########
153	SUPERTRAINING
154	after the loading imposed over prolonged training stages (the long-term TE). The latter of these is analysed more 
155	thoroughly later (sec 6.8).
156	A number of qualitative forms of the cumulative TE (acute or delayed) are distinguished, depending on the 
157	organisation of the training loads (Fig 6.26). Thus, the accumulation can be transient (the body’s immediate 
158	reaction to a complex of training influences of different emphasis, imposed in one or mixed workouts, as well as 
159	the prolonged, parallel use of loading of different emphasis), accumulated (the stratification of traces of the 
160	training loads of different emphasis, following in a certain order in prolonged training stages), and finally, 
161	positive or negative (if the traces of some loads create or, conversely, do not create favourable conditions for 
162	adaptation to other loading).
163	Figure 6.26 The relationship between the different types of training effect. (Siff & Verichoshansky, 1999).
164	At first glance, this classification of the TE may appear to be somewhat tedious. However, its basis is the 
165	dependence of the athlete’s state of fitness on the training loads under actual sporting conditions and it is 
166	impossible not to take its complexity into account when programming training.
167	The physiological nature of the TE is so complex and the forms in which it occurs so diverse that exhaustive 
168	analysis of its characteristics is possible only on the basis of the criteria identified earlier. This has great practical 
169	significance, since the programming of training loads should be based primarily on the objective of achieving a 
170	definite TE. Therefore, a clear understanding of the required TE and the conditions necessary for its achievement 
171	is essential for determining the contents and organisation of training.
172	6.9.2 Factors determ ining the Training Effect
173	In order to select the optimal training loads from the many possible variations, it is necessary to undertake a 
174	preliminary assessment of their effectiveness. To do this, it is useful to analyse the physical effects of the loading 
175	in terms of characteristics such as its contents, volume and organisation (Fig 6.27). The degree of reliability 
176	providing the effect generated by each of these characteristics has great significance for the success of the 
177	training.
178	Figure 6.27 Factors concerned with producing the training effect. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
179	We will examine in more detail the basis for a particular selection associated with each characteristic. In doing so, 
180	we will focus our attention on loading intended to develop explosive-strength and specific endurance.
181	355
182	
183	
184	######## PDF 367 (printed 356) ########
185	SUPERTRAINING
186	The programming of training begins with the determination of its contents, i.e. the composition of the means, 
187	selected on the basis of preliminary assessments using two criteria, namely the specificity of the training load and 
188	the training potential (see Fig 6.27).
189	Specificity of the Load
190	The specificity of the training means refers to their similarity to competition activities regarding motor structure 
191	(including movement patterns), regime of work and mechanism of energy production. This particular criterion is 
192	used to distinguish between means of special and general physical preparedness (SPP and GPP). The SPP means 
193	primarily are for increasing the specific work capacity, whereas the GPP means arc used for general physical 
194	development, for activating restorative processes after prolonged or intense loading, or for facilitating changes 
195	from one type of work to another (Ozolin, 1949; Khomenkov, 1957; Matveyev, 1964).
196	The SPP means should correspond as closely as possible to the dynamics and regime of work of the sports 
197	activity. This requirement is the principle o f dynamic correspondence (discussed in 4.3) which stipulates the 
198	importance of the similarity between the training means and the fundamental sport exercises with respect to the 
199	following indicators (see 4.3):
200	• The amplitude and direction of movement
201	• The accentuated region of force production
202	• The dynamics of the effort (including maximum forcc)
203	• The rate and time of maximum force production
204	• The regime of muscular work.
205	One should, however, take into account that in practice the external similarity of the training means to the 
206	fundamental sport exercise is often overemphasized, whereas the importance of the similarity of the means to the 
207	regime o f muscular work and to the mechanism o f its energy production is underemphasized. It should be noted 
208	that literal similarity of the training means to the fundamental sports activities in motor structure is appropriate 
209	only if it directly improves the athlete's level of physical and technical preparedness (Dyachkov, 1968, 1975).
210	However, for SPP to be effective, it is not so important that the training means precisely mimic the spatial 
211	characteristics of the given exercise. The main criterion of conformity in this case is the regime of muscular work 
212	as a whole. For example, strength exercises such as barbell squats bear little resemblance to the athlete's 
213	movement in running, throwing or playing basketball. However, the use of squats is justified because they 
214	actively contribute to raising the athlete's special work capacity of the appropriate muscles in these sports.
215	An adequate number of SPP means which conform to the fundamental actions is available for training in 
216	every sport. However, it is important to point out that the need to preserve the training potential of the loading 
217	(especially for highly qualified athletes) requires using means that not only conform to, but exceed, competition 
218	conditions, with regard to maximum force, time of maximum force development and the power of the metabolic 
219	processes which determine work-capacity. 
220	On this basis, it is easy to conclude that satisfaction of this 
221	requirement should be associated with improving the strength component of the movement. This emphasis on 
222	strength or, more precisely, the use of specialised strength exercises in the regime of SPP means makes it 
223	necessary to examine this question in more detail.
224	First of all, one must emphasize that the role of strength exercises in sports training is not limited to 
225	enhancing strength alone, as is sometimes thought. It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is 
226	not the fundamental and sole task o f strength training. By itself, the value of maximal strength, in particular, 
227	dwindles and may not sufficiently be utilised in practice for enhancing the effect and specificity of the loading 
228	under actual sporting conditions. However, its role in spced-strength sports is obvious and achieved successfully, 
229	but in many other types of sport (in particular, those requiring endurance), it is still not adequately understood.
230	The development of endurance is associated primarily with using long duration or distance training to 
231	improve aerobic capacity. 
232	However, the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work 
233	invariably is underestimated. It also appears to be forgotten that specialisation of the muscles, as the direct 
234	executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of 
235	endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than 
236	for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning. Therefore, when one uses only the long duration 
237	method for developing endurance, a definite imbalance can arise between the functional level of the
238	6 .9 .3 T he C o n ten ts o f th e Loading
239	
240	
241	######## PDF 368 (printed 357) ########

243	cardiovascular-respiratory systems and the working potential of the muscles. In this case, the anticipated sporting 
244	proficiency will not result.
245	This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in 
246	order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One 
247	needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long 
248	jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which 
249	middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength. Elimination of this insufficiency is possible only 
250	through specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance 
251	training, thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves of 
252	the body. As a result, the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes are enhanced, including ’anaerobic’ 
253	energy production, which provides a high level of local muscular endurance and complements the body's already- 
254	acquired 'aerobic' ability. At the same time, it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in 
255	the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982).
256	Methods of executing specialised strength and jumping exercises in endurance sports should firstly increase 
257	strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing 
258	repeated motor actions. The characteristics of the sport, practical experience and experimentation should 
259	determine the optimal regimes of specialised strength training in each case. The main thing is to overcome the 
260	archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone.
261	The GPP means play no less an important role in the organisation of training. Besides improving traditional 
262	multi-faceted motor coordination and creating a foundation for subsequent specialised motor skill training, some 
263	GPP means can activate the restorative processes. This has special significance in those sports in which there are 
264	few supplementary training means and training is inherently monotonous, i.e. where the competition exercises arc 
265	the basic training means (gymnastics, weightlifting and cyclic sports).
266	For example, research showed that the sole and systematic use of swimming restoration procedures during 
267	the execution of voluminous loading produced an increase of 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength- 
268	endurancc, whereas swimmers who did not use the restorative procedures increased these indicators by only 7.7% 
269	and 4.9% respectively. At the same time, the volume of the training load was increased by an average of 15% 
270	(Kuchnyev, 1977; Platonov, 1980). 
271	In the pre-competition preparation of highly qualified middle-distance 
272	runners, the complex use of low frequency vibromassage and psycho-regulatory training contributed to an 
273	increase in the speed of training distances by 2-4% and to an increase of 12-20% in training volume, executed at 
274	competition speed (Potapchenko, 1979).
275	Thus, the organised combination of training loads and restorative procedures is an important prerequisite for 
276	intensifying and increasing the effectiveness of training. However, it must be emphasized that restoration after 
277	work is a natural process which occurs in a definite sequence over a certain period. This process occurs through 
278	adaptation of interacting physiological systems to stress generated by systematic loading (Yakovlev, 1971). 
279	Artificially accelerating the restoration process as a routine can disturb the natural course of the body's long-term 
280	adaptation to intense muscular activity and therefore can be justified only in clear cases of over-exertion (Siff & 
281	Yessis, 1992).
282	Frequent and regular application of non-specific means of restoration may hinder the adaptation process, 
283	especially when large training loads are used. Increasing the volume and intensity of the loading disturbs 
284	homeostasis as a basic condition for promoting adaptation to loading and enhancement of the restoration 
285	processes. At the same time, premature intervention during the course of restoration can hinder the body's 
286	supercompensatory ability to enhance this process by natural means (Yevgenyev et al, 1975). The interconnected 
287	process of loading-restoration within the general scheme of sports training should be strictly regulated on the 
288	basis of scientific assessment of the athlete's fitness state.
289	Training Potential of the Loading
290	The training potential associated with the loading characterises the extent of its influence on the athlete's fitness. 
291	The higher the training potential relative to the current fitness state, the greater the probability of raising the 
292	athlete's special work capacity. The training potential of the means employed decreases as the special work 
293	capacity increases; therefore, it is important to preserve it by introducing more effective means into the training. 
294	This important principle of organising training is presented in Figure 6.28 (see also 5.4.4). The graph depicts the 
295	practical possibility of altering the athlete's state by using means with different training potential (A, B, C). 
296	However, it is inappropriate to use highly stimulating means prematurely, because the body is functionally

312	6.9.4 The Volume of the Training Load
313	The volume of the training load refers primarily to the quantitative aspects of training and plays an important role 
314	in the long-term adaptation of the body to intense muscular work.
315	The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the 
316	body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the 
317	fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction provoked by individual components of the 
318	training, to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of 
319	the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes o f loading (within 
320	optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity.
321	In types of sports requiring brief, highly concentrated efforts, the volume of loading has yet another 
322	important significance. As discussed earlier, the mechanical integrity o f the ligamentous-joint apparatus can 
323	become the limiting factor to the progress o f sporting performance (see 1.6 and 1.7.2). If these connective tissues 
324	are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the 
325	level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, 
326	high jumping and triple jumping.
327	The volume on its own does not determine the specificity of the training influence of the loading on the body 
328	and the characteristics of the body's adaptive reactions. Therefore, when programming training, the influence of 
329	the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its 
330	duration and intensity. The magnitude of the volume is the quantitative measure of the actual or planned training 
331	load of a certain primary emphasis calculated during each specific microcycle, stage or annual cycle as a whole 
332	(sec 6.2.2).
333	The magnitude o f the volume is determined, first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification. The higher 
334	the qualification, the larger the volume of loading over the year and each stage of preparation. As the athlete's 
335	qualification rises (also within a four-year cycle), so the magnitude, and consequently, the ratio of the loading 
336	volume of different primary emphasis shifts towards an increase in the portion devoted to specialised loading 
337	(Panov, 1975; Zhikharevich, 1976; Vankov, 1977; Matveyev, 1977; Gilyazova, 1978).
338	The magnitude of the annual loading volume is established individually by examining the characteristics of 
339	the athlete's preparation during the preceding stages of training. A more serious task of programming training is 
340	the calculation of the optimal volume of loading in distinct time segments (month, stage or phase). This 
341	magnitude should be determined on the basis of the goals of training during each stage of the annual cycle and 
342	according to the principles of effective organisation of training loads of different primary emphasis, as discussed 
343	in this chapter.

349	The intensity o f the loading determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body or the difficulty 
350	of the training. The intensity regulates the training potential of the given means, the frequency of their use and 
351	the intervals between repeated means or training sessions with large training potential, as well as the ratio of the 
352	volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage. The latter measure 
353	has especially important significance for programming training over prolonged periods, sincc it takes into account 
354	the loading concentration relative to time. Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the 
355	annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1).
356	The duration o f the training load is a vital measure of the volume and must be discussed in more detail, since 
357	it has a significant effect on the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state and can easily be miscalculated by the 
358	average coach.
359	It has already been mentioned that the length of time over which systematic training regimes are employed 
360	(the general volume of loading) has a definite maximum limit, depending on the current adaptation reserves 
361	(CAR) of the body (see 1.16). At the same time, considerable research has established that there is also an upper 
362	limit to the duration of using any specialised training means with a primary emphasis, the exceeding of which is 
363	detrimental to the development of maximum and explosive strength, as well as to the growth of aerobic and 
364	anaerobic capacity. Exceeding this limit does not enhance fitness and wastes die athlete's time and energy. In 
365	programming training, it is important to determine the optimal duration of loading of any primary emphasis, as 
366	well as a suitable rate of increase of the relevant performance indicators.
367	Unfortunately there is no special research directed at determining the optimal length of time for applying 
368	loading of a specific primary emphasis. However, indirect data has been gathered which sheds some light on this 
369	problem. Thus, there is a linear increase in absolute strength in response to a given regime of loading, which 
370	slows down as the limit of this optimal time-span of training is reached, a point which defines exhaustion of the 
371	body's current adaptation energy (see 1.16). Observation of highly qualified athletes indicates that absolute 
372	strength increases with little variation, rising continuously during the year's training.
373	When explosive strength is the purpose of special training, there is a clear tendency for the rise in explosive 
374	strength to slow down; the sharper its growth, the earlier it plateaus. When one is emphasizing the development 
375	of explosive strength exclusively, the plateau appears within 3-4 months. In those cases where explosive strength 
376	is not the key ability (e.g. in a mono-cycle of periodisation in the annual training of decathletes), the increase in 
377	explosive strength can continue (with some fluctuation) for up to 10 months.
378	Loading that is primarily aerobic will produce significant increases in aerobic efficiency even within one 
379	month of training (Borisov, 1979; Sirenko, 1980). The dynamics of the level of aerobic fitness and the indicators 
380	of aerobic loading executed within the aerobic zone (at a HR of 120-170 beats/minute) parallel one another. 
381	Their rate of increase is approximately the same and is linear over a 2-3 months period. Despite increased loading 
382	volume, the aerobic fitness indicators do not increase significantly later on, but fluctuate around the maximum 
383	level achieved (Zatsiorsky et al, 1974; Skorodymova, 1974; Suslov, 1977; Ustkachkintsev, 1979; Sirenko, 1980).
384	About 4 months are necessary to achieve the highest results in anaerobic-glycolytic productivity (Zatsiorsky 
385	ct al, 1974; Serafimova, 1974; Doroshchenko, 1976; Ustkachkintsev, 1979). Increasing the volume of anaerobic 
386	work produces a positive effect only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work, thereby stimulating the 
387	aerobic reaction (Scrafimova, 1974; Naumenko, 1978).
388	Note that the above data applies to the natural conditions of an athlete's preparation, where development of a 
389	given motor ability is achieved together with the execution of other tasks and loading of other primary emphasis. 
390	They conform to those actual loading volumes that highly qualified athletes use according to contemporary 
391	principles of organising training. Since these principles are being constantly refined, the duration of loading 
392	quoted above is not definitive. However, they offer a preliminary guide for the programming of training.
393	6.9.5 The Organisation of Training Loads
394	The organisation of training refers to its regulation over a definite period to ensure attainment of the planned 
395	level of SPP and physical fitness. The basis of such regulation should be the achievement of the positive 
396	cumulative training effect of the loading of different primary emphasis (see Fig 6.26). Here, it is necessary to 
397	observe the chief requirement of maintaining the training potential of the loading. The basic organisational 
398	principles of special strength training, which are discussed in the following sections, are:
399	• The specificity of muscular work

405	• The concentration of loading over time
406	• The separation of strength load, speed development and perfection of technique
407	• Utilisation of the Long-term Training Effect
408	The organisation of loading is defined by two criteria, namely the nature of its distribution over time and the 
409	interrelation between the loads of different primary emphasis.
410	The distribution o f the training load over time refers to the way in which it is organised in separate stages, 
411	cycles and phases of the annual cycle. The distribution of the general volume of loading and its dynamics in the 
412	annual cycle are determined by the traditional periodisation of training and the characteristics of the body's long­
413	term adaptation to training. If one speaks of loading of one primary emphasis, then one must distinguish between 
414	two ways of organising it, namely distributed loading and concentrated loading (see 6.6.1 and Fig 6.23). The first 
415	assumes a relatively uniform distribution of means during an annual cycic; the second, the concentration of 
416	means over definite training stages.
417	The effectiveness of the distribution and concentration methods of organising training loads should be based 
418	on the athlete's level of qualification. Research indicates that both methods arc successful in training athletes of 
419	medium qualification. 
420	The concentrated loading method is appropriate for the training of highly qualified 
421	athletes. In this regard, it has been shown that distribution o f glycolytic work over the annual cycle o f highly 
422	qualified sprinters raises the loading volume, but does not increase the effectiveness o f the loading. However, by 
423	concentrating the volume of glycolytic work at certain stages, the work can be executed at a smaller volume but 
424	with a more significant improvement in speed-endurance (Kornelyuk, 1980). Similar results have been obtained 
425	by concentrating the volume of special strength work of sprinters (Levchenko, 1986), middle-distance runners 
426	(Sirenko & Zhdanovich, 1982), boxers (Filimonov, 1979) and jumpers (Mironenko & Antonova, 1981).
427	The above research has shown that concentration o f the volume o f uni-directional loading produces more 
428	extensive functional changes and greater improvement in the athlete's physical fitness. 
429	The regular use of 
430	training with distributed loading which is dispersed over a prolonged period evokes only a transient functional 
431	reaction which does not enhance the development of long-term adaptation. Distributed loading initially can yield 
432	some rise in functional level but its training potential soon drops because of rapid adaptation of the body to the 
433	training stimuli.
434	The use of loads of different primary emphasis produces the required cumulative training effect, provided 
435	that they arc combined logically over time, since the cumulative loading with means o f different primary 
436	emphasis can have positive or negative effects. Thus, to develop explosive strength, a positive cumulative effect 
437	on the body may be achieved by use of the following brief combinations of training means:
438	• short and long jumping exercises
439	• barbell exercises and jumping exercises
440	• barbell exercises with 30% and 90% of maximum
441	• barbell exercises and the plyomctric method of developing explosivc-strength
442	• leaping with kettle-bells and jumping exercises
443	• barbell exercises and leaping with kettle-bclls.
444	In a single training session the order of the above means, combined in a systematic complex is fairly unimportant, 
445	since the length of time for which the body maintains the after-effect of training stress exceeds the duration of the 
446	workout. During this session and the subsequent restoration period, a generalised summation of the after-effects 
447	of the entire complex of training influences of different primary emphasis occurs, which produces the same 
448	cumulative effect, generally regardless of their sequence. However, it is still sensible to apply the recommended 
449	scheme of Figure 1.7 to minimise the risk of reducing skill and safety.
450	Thus, concerning the development o f explosive strength, the order o f the means is not fundamentally as 
451	important as the volume o f the loading and the degree o f contrast between the different training means. 
452	Nevertheless, one should still preserve the above order of combining means in each case, since this provides the 
453	favourable effect of a brief rise in fitness state, which the first exercise produces as the second one is executed 
454	(see Ch 5.3). The best way of using the above combination of special strength exercises is to employ them 
455	sequentially with active rest between each series. When repeating such a series, it is desirable to vary the exer­
456	cises to avoid monotony and to maintain the optimal rest interval for facilitating recovery.
457	One cannot speak with similar certainty about the effect of the interaction of loading of different primary 
458	emphasis on the development of endurance. Research findings arc inadequate and arc often so contradictory that

472	processes during the short duration activity of strength, strength-speed and strength-endurance sports. Moreover, 
473	no research has analysed the energy processes occurring while the general activity is undoubtedly aerobic, but the 
474	postural muscles are strongly contracted, a situation which suggests that aerobic processes can be strongly active 
475	at a general level while anaerobic processes can also be strongly evident at a local level. This obviously poses a 
476	major problem for the prescription of sport specific training.
477	It is to be hoped that in the near future the negative consequences of such interpretations will be eliminated, 
478	but until then it should be noted that current experimental data indicates that a positive interaction of endurance 
479	loading occurs when:
480	• aerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training
481	• aerobic exercises are done after glycolytic-anaerobic training (in small volume)
482	• glycolytic-anaerobic exercises are done after ATP-CP training.
483	Under these conditions the previous loading creates favourable conditions for executing the subsequent loading 
484	and raises the effect of the training session as a whole.
485	There is a negative interaction when (Volkov, 1975):
486	• ATP-CP exercises are done after a large amount of any glycolytic work
487	• glycolytic-anaerobic exercises follow large volumes of aerobic work.
488	It has been established that restoration of energy resources and disturbance of endocrinc equilibrium within the 
489	body is prolonged by 2-3 days after a large volume of aerobic work. During this period it is appropriate to 
490	employ a small volume of anacrobic loading which will not negatively influence the restoration of aerobic 
491	capacity and will stimulate the development of anaerobic capacity.
492	Restoration after moderate volumes of anaerobic loading usually takes 3-8 hours. 
493	However, very large 
494	volumes of anaerobic loading will delay restoration. The training effect of ATP-CP workouts deteriorates if the 
495	sessions are done without allowing full restoration from the preceding loading (Nabatnikova, 1972; Volkov, 
496	1975; Platonov, 1980).
497	Sequential accumulation of the training effect of loading of different primary emphasis has a place in long­
498	term preparation and is achieved by the action of preceding work on subsequent work. 
499	In this case, if the 
500	preceding work creates favourable circumstances for the subsequent work, there is a positive accumulation of 
501	their training effects.
502	For the development of explosive strength, positive accumulation is achieved by means of a sequence which 
503	applies extensive (i.e. high volume) training with submaximal resistance first, followed by explosive training. In 
504	this case the positive accumulation is achieved by the first loading regime producing a rise in the general energy 
505	potential of the neuromuscular system. This creates favourable conditions for further adaptation, facilitated by the 
506	subsequent loading and emphasis on developing the athlete's ability to display great explosive power. The reverse 
507	sequence of this loading scheme leads to a negative cumulative effect.
508	The mechanism of sequential accumulation is appropriate only if the training effect of the previous work has 
509	become relatively stable, which takes at least 4-6 weeks. When the strength means of different emphasis are 
510	changed over shorter time intervals, for example after 2 weeks, the body cannot differentiate between the 
511	specifics of their individual influence and the body's adaptive reaction as mediated by the transient accumulation 
512	process. Thus, a change after 2-week stages of use in the order of loading of different emphasis minimally alters 
513	the resulting training effect.
514	With the development of special endurance (i.e. the main aim of cyclic sports), the sequential accumulation 
515	of the training cffcct of loading of different primary emphasis displays a more complex character than the 
516	development of explosive strength, which leads to the following conclusions:

531	training means, which may not always be appropriate for highly qualified athletes (Platonov, 1980).
532	The methods of developing endurance were established long ago and there are still two opposing viewpoints. One 
533	of these is based on the value of concurrent development of general and special endurance (Matveyev, 1970; 
534	Ogoltsov, 1971; Nabatnikova, 1972). This variant introduces special endurance loading right from the beginning 
535	of the preparatory period, during which one is also developing general endurance. It is assumed that this training 
536	will be more specialised, creating more favourable conditions for specific adaptation to competitive activities. 
537	This point of view has been corroborated experimentally, much of the research having been done with athletes 
538	who had not yet reached the highest levels of sports mastery, in particular with junior middle-distance runners 
539	(Baranov, 1969), swimmers (Kuzovenkov, 1969) and skiers (Malikov, 1974).
540	The viewpoint emphasizes the sequential development of endurance, where one begins by enhancing 
541	cardiovascular capability, followed by anaerobic-glycolytic endurance, and finally, short-term endurance (the 
542	creatine phosphate process). The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-eftect of 
543	anaerobic work (Ozolin, 1959, 1970; Volkov, 1963; Yakovlev, 1957; Borisov, 1979; Loktev, 1978). A gradual 
544	increase in the duration of cardiovascular loading leads to an accumulation of energy substrates and an increase in 
545	the body's energy potential (Yakovlev, ct al, 1960). Here, the intensity of loading, rather than its volume is of 
546	principal significance (Astrand & Rodahl, 1970). When one's cardiovascular ability is insufficient, an excessive 
547	increase in the volume of anaerobic means causes a decrease in sporting performance (Naumenko, 1978; 
548	Vavilov, 1977; Scrafimova, 1974; Morzhevikov, 1980).
549	A third viewpoint on endurance development has been formulated and experimentally verified. Basically, it 
550	involves the increase in volume of concurrent aerobic and anaerobic training means, but with a sequential change 
551	in emphasis from general to special endurance. The effectiveness of this type of training construction in the 
552	annual cycle has been demonstrated, in particular, for highly qualified middle-distance runners (Doroshchenko, 
553	1976; Loktev, 1978; Borisov, 1979), as well as for multi-year training (Linyets, 1979). One can assume that this 
554	system represents a compromise which combines the benefits of concurrent and sequential special endurance 
555	training.
556	The organisation of loading is closely associated with selecting the optimal rest interval between repetitions 
557	in a single training session and between succcssive sessions. It is vital to remember that the essence of training 
558	consists not only of muscular work, but also of the effect of the adaptive reaction elicited by it. Therefore, ihe 
559	rest pause is actually a training means which is just as important as muscular work, so that it should be 
560	employed skillfully. It has been emphasized repeatedly that the art of training management consists of the 
561	systematic combination of specific and non-specific loading, together with careful regulation of work and rest 
562	stages (Hippenreitor, 1955; Petrovsky, 1969; Ozolin, 1949, 1966). The rest interval is one of the most important 
563	components of training methodology. Devising the optimal pause between repetitions and other stages of training 
564	work requires extensive methodological competence and practical skill in utilising this pause effectively.
565	These findings highlight the extremely complex connection between the athlete's state and the training load, 
566	and coupled with this, the difficulty of selecting the optimal method of training organisation to achieve the 
567	desired special work capacity. Nevertheless, despite the paucity of data, which does not allow one to prescribe 
568	exact recommendations for each sport, some principal guidelines for organising annual training loads may be 
569	identified, as given in various sections of this text.

579	Considerable research (Nikitin, 1977; Mironenko, 1979; Antonova, 1982; Levchenko, 1982) has revealed a 
580	steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 
581	weeks). This decrease is the result of voluminous strength loading (Figure 6.29, shaded rectangle), after which 
582	speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it. Since this phenomenon does not agree with 
583	established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness as an essential condition for 
584	effective organisation of training, and since it is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining, it has become 
585	a subject of special study. The results of this study occupy the remainder of this section.
586	The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body 
587	reacts with diminished response. There is a characteristically simple connection between the quantity of work and 
588	the dynamics of the athlete’s fitness state.

590	An increase in volume of loading raises the athlete's special work-capacity, whereas a decrease lowers it. If the 
591	volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the 
592	volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, 
593	however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work- 
594	capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE) which accompanies one of 
595	the forms of adaptation to volume of loading.
596	This phenomenon has been known for some time in practice, where it has been observed as an increase in 
597	performance in several sports after a decrease in the volume of the training load during the pre-competition stage 
598	(Ozolin, 1949, 1967; Dyachkov, 1953; Matveyev, 1970; Charycv, 1975). However, this reflects only the external 
599	evidence of this type of adaptation, and the physiological conditions, mechanisms and characteristics of the 
600	LDTE until recently have not been a subject of much research. Essentially, no one expected that the existence of 
601	the LDTE offered any great promise for systematising training, especially for highly qualified athletes.
602	The LDTE phenomenon of concentrated strength loading has also been observed in several cyclic sports, 
603	including middle-distance running (Zhdanovich, 
604	1980), swimming (Rudokenc, 1981) and ice-skating

610	phenomenon is the increase in volume of intense distance work, which impairs the ability to produce explosive 
611	strength, because the latter plays a non-specific role in cyclic sports. Based on research and experience, the 
612	LDTE phenomenon may be characterised as follows (sec Fig 6.31):
613	1. Concentration of the volume of strength loading (A) over a limited period exerts an extensive, unidirectional

629	5. The length of time for which the LDTE is displayed is determined by the volume and duration of the 
630	concentrated strength loading. In principle, the duration of the LDTE (T2) is approximately equal to the 
631	duration of the strength training stage (T 1). Under the actual training conditions o f highly qualified athletes, 
632	the LDTE was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation. 
633	However, one should bear in mind that appearance of the LDTE is individualised and to a large degree 
634	depends on the athlete's volume of loading and individual recuperative ability. An equivalent volume of 
635	loading for two athletes of the same qualification can yield significantly different effects.
636	There are a number of important circumstances associated with the production and use of the LDTE of strength 
637	loading during the annual cycle. Athletes invariably do not allow or do not have sufficient time for recuperation 
638	after extensive strength loading. Consequently, they minimise the possibility of stimulating a LDTE of strength 
639	loading and thereby maintain conditions which are extremely stressful for the body. Besides this, the body is 
640	regularly forced to unjustifiably deplete its current adaptation energy and sometimes draw upon its deep 
641	adaptation energy to restore its energy potential. Consequently, the effectiveness o f preparation is fairly low 
642	under such conditions and special work-capacity is not very high during the competition stage.
643	During the period of emergence of the LDTE of extensive strength loading, it is relatively easy and painless 
644	for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work. This is manifested in 
645	the slowed or even decreased growth of spced-strength. The volume of training work, therefore, should not be 
646	increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE. One should be especially cautious with strength loading 
647	during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small 
648	volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved

654	level of speed-strcngth preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of 
655	strength loading.
656	At this point it is relevant to comment on the relationship between strength training and technical training, 
657	especially since it has often been stressed that there seems to be no logical connection between these types of 
658	training. It should be noted that the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the 
659	most specific o f all the special training means. Therefore, this special means of training should be viewed 
660	simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training and should occupy a placc of central importance in 
661	the training programme. In other words, a strength training programme should first be constructed in accordance 
662	with the principle of gradual increase in intensity and secondly, be combined with technique training so as to 
663	peak concurrently with the competitive act, performed with maximal effort.
664	At the highest level of sports mastery, improvement in performance is determined primarily by increasing the 
665	athlete’s special work capacity, which is essential for improving proficiency in any competitive event. Technical 
666	mastery is the ability to effectively realise one’s motor potential under competitive conditions. Increasing the 
667	level of special work capacity, in particular one’s strength potential, in turn, promotes improvement in technique. 
668	This is largely a result of the athlete becoming able to concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of 
669	movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular 
670	control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue. 
671	Thus, special physical preparation and 
672	technical training are closely linked and interdependent. However, the dominant role in this interaction is played 
673	by special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training.
674	It should never be forgotten that high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one’s current level of speed- 
675	strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level 
676	athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. 
677	Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the conccntrated volume of 
678	strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength. 
679	Technique rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less 
680	likelihood of reinforcing errors which may arise in connection with the body's lowered functional state, caused by 
681	high-volume loads. 
682	This type of programming, especially as part of the conjugate system of training, 
683	successively introduces different modes of loading into the training rather than separating them in time, so that 
684	each mode tends to gradually replace its predecessor.

686	With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents 
687	occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training 
688	under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude. Here, characteristics of the LDTE phenomenon have been 
689	observed in swimmers, with significant increases being measured in maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume 
690	of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactatc accu­
691	mulation (Vaitsekhovsky et al, 1974). These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at

699	diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP.
700	The stay at low-oxygen (hypobaric) conditions common to both experiments provided a very demanding 
701	training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body’s homeostasis and subsequent activation of

741	As has already been emphasized, knowledge of the characteristics of the interdependence between the dynamics 
742	of the athlete's fitness state and the training loads is of central importance in programming training. However, in 
743	practice, there is very little research concerning the dynamics of the athlete's state over the annual cycle.

6.8.3 The Structure of Special Physical Preparedness
The above-mentioned characteristics of functional specialisation in multi-year training are associated with 
specific adaptive changes in the cardiovascular-respiratory and neuromuscular systems, as well as in the 
efficiency of the central nervous mechanisms that regulate their activities. For many years, it was not appreciated 
that each type of sport requires not only a distinct type of motor skill, but also a different type of physiological 
fitness. Even today, the role and nature of supplementary training is not clearly understood. For example, much 
the same sort of resistance training may be prescribed for many different athletes in various sports, simply 
because the sports seem to be superficially similar. 
It must be realised that supplementary or 'cross' training 
cannot simply be used in a very general way in the belief that strength, speed or endurance acquired in one 
situation will be of direct benefit to performance in another situation.
For example, muscle endurance gained through supplementary running training does not mean that it will 
directly improve the performance of a competitive rower or cyclist. Special physical preparedness (SPP) depends 
on developing the necessary physiological qualities with the same muscles and neuromuscular mechanisms that 
are encountered in the given sport. Therefore, training for special physical preparedness must be based on a 
thorough understanding of the different types of specificity discussed in 1.3 and the characteristics of the 
interaction between the various organs and the neuromuscular system, which determines the change in special 
work capacity.
It was also assumed that one could develop each fitness quality separately with some or other form of general 
training, then assemble all of them to produce the necessary sport specific fitness from them. The emergence of 
specificity from an array of non-specific fitness qualities, however, is not supported by current physiological and 
biochemical research, so it is clear that the management of training must take into consideration the effects of 
concurrent and sequential training means. Therefore, the problem of programming training was examined from 
several different positions in earlier chapters (see especially 3.2.1 regarding speed and quickness, and 4.4 
regarding general endurance).
6.9 Preparedness and the Training Load
The connection between the athlete's fitness state and a given loading regime is the central issue in the theory and 
practice of programming training (sec 6.3). It is also the weakest link in the management of training, which 
requires the special attention of scientists and coaches. Before examining the practical aspects of the connection 
between loading and the athlete's fitness state, the concepts of training load and training effect must be defined 
more thoroughly (see Fig 6.12).
Strictly speaking, the training load does not exist as an independent entity. Terminologically, it must be 
distinguished from the load used in weight training, which refers to the resistance or force imposed on the body 
by a weight or machinc. Training load is related to the muscular work which the body must produce to carry out 
a given regime of exercise in training or competition. More precisely, muscular work is that training potential 
which elicits an appropriate training effect from the body. Thus, the training potential of muscular work, and 
consequently its training effect is to a large extent determined by the athlete’s current fitness state.
It should be clear that the interrelation between the athlete's fitness state and the training load is extremely 
complex, dependent upon many factors and determined by numerous variables (see Fig 6.12). Unfortunately, 
research concerning this connection is limited and often contradictory. 
Therefore, this chapter attempts to 
systematise and examine the connection between the athlete's fitness state and the training load, drawing largely 
upon the results of extensive research by Verkhoshansky and his co-workers.
6.9.1 The Training Load and its Effect
The training load refers to the quantitative calculation of the training work performed. It is customary to 
recognise the concepts of external, internal and psychological loading, i.e. the quantity of work done, its effect on 
the body and the psychologically perceived effect on the athlete, respectively (Matveyev, 1964; Volkov, 1969; 
Ozolin, 1970; Tumanyan, 1974). Volume and intensity are used as the most general characteristics of the training 
load, as defined in 6.2.2 (Ozolin, 1949; Matveyev, 1956; Khomenkov, 1970; Nabatnikova, 1972).
There are other classifications of the training load based on the motor characteristics of the sport, the power 
of muscular work^ the pedagogical tasks of the training, the effect on restoration, the effect on subsequent work, 
the interaction of work regimes of different emphasis (e.g. the interaction of primarily strength work and speed-
352


######## PDF 364 (printed 353) ########
SUPERTRAINING
strength work) and other criteria (Farfel, 1958; Volkov, 1969, 1974; Zimkin, 1963; Monogarov & Platonov, 
1975; Suslov, 1978; Scherrer, 1962, 1969).
However, each of these classifications, applied separately, are not quite suitable for resolving the task of the 
programming of training. A somewhat different approach is required here, which provides special requirements 
for the preliminary assessment of the loading and takes into account the above classification criteria.
The concept of loading suggests firstly a physiological measure of the effect of specialised muscular work on 
the body, reflected in the form of specific functional reactions. Consequently the necessity arose, in developing 
the concepts of external and internal loading, for introducing the concepts of the training potential of the loading 
and its training effect to enable one to more precisely describe the relationship between cause and effect (see 6.3, 
especially Fig 6.12).
The influence of the loading is expressed by its training effect (TE), assessed, first of all, by the magnitude of 
the change in the athlete's fitness state. 
Research concerning the forms in which the TE occurs is very 
contradictory, generally amounting to the following representation of events in the training process (Zatsiorsky, 
1964; Volkov, 1966; Matveyev, 1977):
Acute TE > Delayed TE > Cumulative TE.
The first two forms are associated with the single training session: the acute TE is the body’s current reaction to 
the physical loading, while the delayed TE is the alteration in the athlete's state observed some time after the 
workout. The cumulative TE is the result of the subsequent accumulation of all the TEs that were elicited during 
training.
However, the above scheme is one-sided and does not take into account the qualitative changes in the TE 
when they are produced by training loads of different primary emphasis (e.g. on strength, speed-strength or 
muscle endurance). The fact is that the accumulation of training effects is not simply a summation of separate 
effects, but a synergistic whole (i.e. the sum of the parts is greater than the whole).
The mechanism of generalised adaptation as a universal quality of a biological system establishing a balance 
between its state and external conditions, is determined primarily by the automatic selection of an accommodative 
strategy which is most appropriate in that situation. This involves selective response to the training influences of 
different primary emphasis and their stable integration into a well-adapted system. 
As has already been 
mentioned, the cumulative TE itself can have a different quantitative and qualitative expression, depending on 
factors including the current state of fitness, the order in which training regimes of different emphasis follow each 
other, the after-effects of preceding loading, and the duration of given training means (Verkhoshansky, 1970).
For example, it has long been known that the result of a workout depends on the sequence of exercises (e.g. 
with primary emphasis on speed, strength or endurance). Considerable research has shown clearly the effect of a 
particular sequence of training loads of different emphasis during long-term training on the body, e.g. 'aerobic' 
and 'anaerobic' glycolytic loading for developing special endurance (Nabatnikova, 1972; Volkov, 1975; Platonov, 
1980) or strength and jumping exercises for explosive strength (Tatyan, 1975; Khodykin, 1976; Chemousov, 
1978; Levchenko, 1980).
Based on similar research, it has been suggested that a distinction be made between the concepts of partial 
TE (the result of the effect of loading of one primary emphasis or means) and cumulative TE (the result of the 
generalised effect on the body of loading of different primary emphasis, applied concurrently or sequentially). In 
the latter case there are both quantitative and qualitative aspects to the TE. The distinction between these 
concepts can best be explained by examples.
In one experiment (Fig 6.24), group 1 began by using barbell exercises, followed by depth-jumps (a 
plyometric method of developing explosive strength). Group 2 used the reverse sequence of means. Each group 
of means were used for three months each. Group 3 used the barbell exercises and the depth-jumps concurrently 
throughout both 3-month stages. The overall volume of the loading was equivalent in all groups.
The results of the studies enabled us first of all to compare the partial TE of utilising only barbell exercises 
and depth-jumps (the first stage for groups 1 and 2), as well as the cumulative TE obtained as a result o f two 
different ways of organising the loading: concurrent (group 3) and sequential (the second stage of groups 1 and 
2). The following conclusions were derived from this experiment:
1. The partial TE of the depth-jumping is greater than that of the barbell exercises.
