999	
1000	######## PDF 301 (printed 290) ########
1001	SUPERTRAJNINC
1002	• Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training
1003	• Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before.
1004	In another study (Fig 5.14), qualified athletes modelled different variants of weightlifting pre-competition training 
1005	under laboratory conditions (Deniskin, 1976). A leg extension movement involving the lifting of a 1RM was used 
1006	as a model, starting with an initial knee angle of 90°. The training effect o f the plyometric method (with depth- 
1007	jumps) was investigated after a fust stage of intensive work with resistance, the purpose of which was to increase 
1008	explosive strength. Only depth-jumps were used during the sccond and third stages. The necessity for having two 
1009	such stages was dictated by the results of a preliminary investigation which showed that the rise in functional 
1010	state achieved after one stage is unstable. The fourth stage served as a control and served only to test 
1011	performance. The subjects were given a complete rest between stages to enhance supercompensation.
1012	The experiment showed that the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of 
1013	explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training. This demonstrates the use of these means in 
1014	two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises 
1015	the level of special fitness. 
1016	There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete 
1017	rest following the first and sccond stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not 
1018	a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of 
1019	passive or activc rest.
1020	Several researchers have studied the systematic use of special strength training by highly qualified athletes 
1021	under various training conditions (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin). It was established that using electromuscular 
1022	stimulation (ES) first, followed by plyometrics yielded a larger training effect than the use of these means in the 
1023	reverse order. However, a significantly larger training effect was obtained by using them together during the same 
1024	stage, when, for example, ES and plyomctrics are applied concurrently with heavy resistance exercises. When the 
1025	training is not chiefly for strength, ES and plyometrics were observed to have the lowest effect during periods of 
1026	complete or partial rest.

1028	in the accompanying text. Ss » starting strength, Se = explosive strength, Fmax = maximum force, and tmax 53 time taken to reach

1036	Unidirectional emphasis on qualities such as strength or endurance may be used not only in individual worko 
1037	but also during each microcycle (Kudelin, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1980). Research has sho 
1038	that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is 
1039	gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle. Moreover, the effectiveness of the conjugate 
1040	sequence system with advanced athletes is such that the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as 
1041	much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration o f specific adaptation (see 5.4.2).
1042	However, it must be noted that unidirectional loading is effective only if one uses a diverse complcx of means 
1043	with a single primary emphasis, together with a variety of training methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov &. 
1044	Monograov, 1977; Verkhoshansky, 1977). Furthermore, an important condition for implementing concentrated 
1045	loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, sincc the frequent use of these means already intensifies the 
1046	training. In this context, the loading may be considered concentrated if its volume in the month in which it is 
1047	applied constitutes 23-25% of the general volume for the year.
1048	The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the 
1049	potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on 
1050	heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill 
1051	or speed. Since the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect, a diminished 
1052	loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to 
1053	supercompensate to the desired level o f preparedness. The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated 
1054	blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 
1055	weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without 
1056	adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training 
1057	effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training.
1058	5.4 The Principal Aims of Special S trength Training

loading over the annual cycle.
Accompanying the growth of proficiency of non-elite athletes, the fitness state shows a trend towards 
regularity which reflects the type of training periodisation used during the annual cycle. During monocyclic 
periodisation (e.g. in the decathlon) the level of spccial-strength preparedness generally increases without any 
significant fluctuations throughout the year. In bi-cyclic periodisation, two large waves are clearly planned which 
conform to two mesocycles of preparation, one ending in the winter and the other in the summer competition.
However, in the case of highly qualified athletes, the dynamics of speed-strength over the annual cycle 
cannot be regulated in such a manner. Research reveals a pronounced diversity in the dynamics of the fitness
366


######## PDF 378 (printed 367) ########
SUPERTRAINING
state of these athletes. 
Large fluctuations in speed-strength preparedness can be o f different duration and 
magnitude, can occur at different stages of the annual cycle and often show neither a logical correlation with 
traditional periodisation of training (for the given sport) nor the competition calendar.
A phenomenon which has great significance for regulating the influence of loading was first discovered by 
observing the dynamics of the functional state over the annual cycle. It was found that the speed-strength o f thigh 
extension, knee extension and plantarflexion can show different trends o f change at certain training stages. The 
dynamics of the explosive strength of triple jumpers serves as an example (Verkhoshansky, 1988). This phe­
nomenon is associated with the relatively unequal emphasis of the training influences on the functioning of the 
muscles which are responsible for movement of the lower extremities. The concurrent use of jumping and barbell 
exercises exerts a more intense local influence on the plantarflexors than other muscles of the lower extremity 
and, consequently, depresses their functional state. However, the loading is not as intense on the thigh extensors, 
so that their functional indicators reflect a high value. In this case, the athlete notices that movement coordination 
is difficult although, on the whole, he feels perfectly fit.
Thus, when one attempts to determine the composition and the means of special strength training without 
taking into account the differences in their primary emphasis on the specific muscle groups producing a sporting 
movement, the result can be that the functional state of the muscles involved does not conform to that required by 
the sport. This, in turn, exerts a negative effect on the quality of the athlete's technical preparation and his 
preparedness for competition. Consequently, in this case, it is necessary to regulate the emphasis of the loading 
on the plantarflexors, and periodically decrease the loading on them, especially during the technical and 
immediate pre-competition training stages.
The athlete’s fitness state, as characterised by his aerobic and anaerobic capabilities, depends on the contents 
and organisation of the training loads. One study which corroborated this finding examined the results of two 
groups of middle-distance runners training with different training programmes over an annual cycle (Sirenko, 
1980). Each group followed a training programme with the same volume and distribution of running means, but 
Group I used a traditional single-peak distribution of strength-means, whereas Group 2 used a double-peaked 
distribution of means with the emphasis concentrated in December and March-April.
Group 2 proved superior in all tests of functional ability, including aerobic efficiency, 'anaerobic threshold' 
(onset of blood lactate accumulation) and the results of control runs of 400m and 1200m, as well as in their 
sporting performances. During the summer competition stage Group 2 improved the 800m time by an average of 
4.8 seconds and the 1500m run by 6.3 seconds, whereas in Group 1, the improvements were 3.4 and 4.6 seconds, 
respectively.
This and other studies of the influence of training loads on functional indicators show that three levels of 
change in an athlete's fitness state during training may be identified:
1. A long-term level characterised by the steady rise in the athlete's special work-capacity. 
This level is 
associated with prolonged training periods of one or more years and its basis lies in long-term adaptation, 
promoted chiefly by the volume of loading.
2. A medium-term level characterised by less stable and readily reversible functional changes, the basis for 
which is compensatory adaptation. These changes are associated with lengthy training stages of up to 5-6 
months and, together with the volume of the load, are produced by the characteristics of its contents, in 
particular, the proportion of intensive means in the total volume of loading.
3. A short-term level characterised by brief, but not precisely measurable, changes in the functional indicators,
i.e. changes representing the body's acute reaction to the training load. These changes concern the micro- 
cycle and are elicited by the magnitude of the load, the intensity of loading, the individual ability of the 
athlete to endure the loading and his restorative capabilities. At this level, the dynamics of the functional 
indicators are largely random and at times unpredictable. This level is not determined by the adaptation of the 
first two levels and is important only for organisation of the microcycle and achievement of the immediate 
effect of the current loading.
One practical conclusion that can be drawn from these findings is that the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state 
during the annual cycle are controllable. The dependence of the dynamics of fitness on the contents, volume and 
organisation of the loading is determined by definite adaptive processes. 
Consequently, training should be 
structured by first of all taking into account the dynamics of the athlete's special physical preparedness (SPP) and 
controlling the degree of conformity of the training to the actual sporting dynamics required at each stage.

SUPERTRAINING
Mastering the ability to effectively programme the contents of training and regulate the dynamics of the athlete’s 
fitness state during training involves eliminating all weak links in the system of managing training and thereby 
significantly increasing the probability of achieving the intended level of sporting performance.
The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary 
level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. 
Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability 
of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller.
6.12 Principles of Programming and Organising Training
The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume 
and organisation of training loads are determined by the objectives of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The 
objectives consist of three main components:
• the desired improvement in performance
• the appropriate changcs in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness
• the necessary modification of special physical preparedness.
In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach, which 
is understood in the following way: if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work 
and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy.
6.12.1 Forms of Constructing Training
Construction of training involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different 
primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a 
minimal expenditure of energy.
Consequently, time and organisation are two closely interdependent variables in the planning of training. 
The contents and organisation of training are dictated by the training objectives and the characteristics of 
adaptation to the intense muscular work deemed to be necessary for the given period. The time limitation 
imposed by the competition calendar and the duration of the energy supply from the current adaptation reserves 
affects the selection of the contents and organisation of training. Actual conditions do not always satisfy the 
optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the 
skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant.
It is appropriate now to examine the different forms of training against a background of research into the 
characteristics of adaptation to intense exercise and the principal trends produced by the given loading in the 
dynamics of the athlete's cxercise state. Two categories of training construction may be identified: one based on 
structural organisation and the other on time management. With respect to organisation, one has to consider the 
ways of combining loading of different primary emphasis as a basic condition for achieving a large training 
effect. With respect to time, one has to consider ways of regulating the loading within definite cycles and stages, 
as determined by the periodisation of training and the competition calendar.
6.12.2 Organisational Aspects of Structuring Training
There are essentially two basic different ways of organising training, namely the complcx and the conccntrated 
loading methods. Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several 
different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a 
given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training.
Complex training refers to the concurrent use of different training means in the same workout, microcycle or 
mesocycle. For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a 
complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during 
different sessions on the same day. If complex means are to be utilised, it is essential to understand fully how the 
different means and exercises interact with one another, as determined by the acute and delayed after-effects of 
each (discussed earlier in this chaptcr). In addition, the prescription of complex means depends on the individual, 
the level of proficiency of the athlete, the specific objective, and the stage of the training programme, especially 
the proximity to important competitions

since they each model different types o f jump (directly upwards versus forwards and upwards). Slow

• Since plyometric actions involve a powerful concentric phase assisted by activation of the muscles by the 
stretch reflex, it is initially useful to improve jumping ability from a static start, without exposing oneself to 
the greater musculotendinous stress of a dynamic start. Standing broad and vertical jumps, with regular 
attempts to increase the distance or height achieved without a preliminary dynamic dip, can be useful in this 
regard. The usual vertical jump test may be used as one of the exercises, progressing from a static flexed 
knee start to a dynamic dip start with arms flung vigorously upwards. 
To gain an idea of individual 
progress, the power developed may be calculated from the Lewis nomogram or from the formula: Power P
= (21.693) b Vh watts, where B = bodymass in kg and H = height jumped in metres.
As eccentric, isometric and concentric strength increases in individual exercises over the range commonly used for 
the plyometric activities, the athlete may progress to actions which more rapidly integrate all three aspects of 
piyomctric movement. Although lower body plyometric actions have been referred to above in the form of 
dcpth-jumps, the same principles may be applied to upper body impulsive methods with medicine ball catching 
ind throwing, plyometric press-ups, plyometric bench-presscs and similar actions using loaded swings or other 
specialised apparatus.
The training effect of depth-jumps or shock-loading for developing explosive strength is very large, having 
bttle equal when compared with the other means of strength training, especially when combined in a complex with 
other forms of intensive strength training. This has been corroborated by a number of studies (Semyenov, 1971; 
Tatyan, 1974; Dobrovolsky, 1972; Savin, 1974; Khodykin, 1974; Deniskin, 1976), the results o f which are 
discussed further in several articles (Papysheva, 1967; Kharabuga, 1967; Cheryeshneva, 1967; Kuznetsov, 1970; 
Burla, 1973; Press, 1974). The plyometric method of developing explosive strength already occupies a firm place 
a athletics and is used by many distinguished athletes.
It is interesting to note that depth landings (i.e. depth jumps without the rebound after landing) alone can also 
have a significant cffcct on concentric and eccentric strength. This was shown by Durscnev and Raevsky (1978) 
who investigated the effect of depth landings from heights of 2m or more onto soft gymnastic mats. Under these 
conditions, the subjects acquired the ability to display brief muscle tension (over periods of between 0.028-0.061 
secs) of magnitude 1500-3500 kgf, i.e. over 20 times bodyweight for heights of up to 3.2 metres. The rationale for 
using this method was that weight training or other similar methods of resistance training cannot produce this 
intensity of voluntary effort.
It was found that the maximum possible height which the athletes could contemplate using produced the 
greatest increase in strength, although they often hesitated to attempt these extremely stressful jumps. It should 
be pointed out that the drop heights studied were for experimental purposes alone and it would be most 
inadvisable to use drops of 3.2 metres for training. It appeared that the main consideration for enhancing strength 
isnot the type of muscle contraction, but the intensity and speed of contraction elicited by the exercise. The high 
nsk of overload injury associated with falling from great heights should always be borne in mind, so it is 
important to increase the drop height gradually from fairly low levels, to limit the number of drops per session, to 
iand on suitably firm shock-absorbing surfaces and to pay careful attention to landing technique.
The plyometric method of developing explosive strength and reactive ability solves to a significant degree the 
problem of economising training, since it ensures that a high level of special conditioning is attained in the 
minimum time. Thus, a comparative experiment revealed that a group of track-and-field jumpers executing 
primarily depth-jumps (all of them did 475 jumps) over a 12 week period in the preparation phase showed greater 
improvement in reactive ability than the group which trained with traditional methods and executed 1472 general 
push-offs (squats, jumping and hopping with a barbell weighing 90-95%, 70-80% and 30-40% of 1RM) and lifted 
i total volume of 93 tons! Carefully periodised training programmes which combine resistance exercises with 
plyomctrics can develop explosive strength even more effectively than plyometrics alone, provided the resistance 
movements precede the plyometric activities in individual sessions.
The use of many repetitions and sets of plyometric drills in an attempt to facilitate adaptation to cope with 
exhaustive bouts of stretch-shortening activities such as rebounding in basketball is not supported by research 
(Nicol et al, 1997). Instead any improvement in such situations is better mediated by the use of training to 
enhance movement efficiency. This is a very important point which concerns all explosive and ballistic activities:

have resulted from the separate non-systematic use of these same means, even at increased volume. Experimental 
assessment of the cumulative effects of different variations of the combination of means is necessary for applying 
the complex system of special strength training means.
A number of researchers, including Purvin, FChodykin, Dcniskin, Tatian and Chemousov have studied the 
systematic use of special strength means in speed-strength sports. They have established that the sequence of 
means in the preparatory period (beginning with strength, then speed-strength means, or vice-versa) has no real 
significance for novices. Consequently, the same effect can be obtained by using these means in any order.
A relatively larger effect than produced by the above-mentioned variants (with the same volume of training 
load) occun-ed in groups who used strength and speed-strength means concurrently by alternating them in mixed 
training sessions. This alternation sequence creates the optimal conditions for functional adaptation. This docs 
not ignore the fact that this training regime, with a rest interval between sessions on the same day, also produces a 
positive response of the after-effect phenomenon by use of the strength and speed-strength exercises. On the 
whole, this elicitcd more intense and more stable adaptation. It should be noted that the contrasting of stimuli in 
mixed workouts by alternating training means which are primarily of a strength and speed-strength character 
undoubtedly has a positive effect.
In another experiment one group of novice athletes used weights exercises in the first stage of training and 
plyometric depth jumps in the next stage. A second group did the same exercises in reverse order and a third 
group did these same exercises together in both stages, although not in the same workout. It was established that 
the first variant was more effective for developing speed-strength. The concurrent use of exercises (the third 
variant) caused significant improvement in speed-strength in the first stage, but the rate of improvement in speed- 
strength decreased noticeably in the second stage, due to monotonous repetition. The second variant (reversed use 
of these same means) produced significant improvement after the first stage due to the larger training effect of the 
plyometric method. However, the acquired speed-strength qualities were lowest at the end o f the second stage.
Another experiment studied the question of whether the execution of speed-strength exercises in one workout 
against the background of the positive after-effect produced by previous tonic strength work influences the 
effectiveness of speed-strength preparation of novices. One group of athletes executed exercises in this sequence 
(i.e. strength, then speed-strcngth work) during the fundamental stage of their workouts, while another group did 
the reverse. The pauses between exercises were increased slightly to minimise the influence of the positive after­
effect of the preceding work on the subsequent work. A third group executed depth jumps. The presence of this 
group in the experiment served two purposes: firstly, to study the effectiveness of plyometrics and secondly, to 
compare this effect with the results obtained with a complcx of less effective means. There was no statistically 
significant difference in speed-strength of the subjects in the first two groups. The largest increase in all the 
parameters of the control movement was discovered in the third group.
Thus, an increase in the training effect of speed-strength exercises performed against the background of the 
positive after-effect of strength work has not been corroborated in the training of novices. In this experiment, the 
means with a higher training effect (i.e. dcpth-jumps) produced significantly larger improvement in speed-strength 
fitness for a smaller volume of training. In explaining these results, one should take into account that any training 
influence will leave significant traces in an untrained person. The body is unable to react selectively to a chiefly 
strength or speed-strength means in one workout. In addition, the period over which the traces of the training 
stimulus are maintained is apparently longer than the duration of the after-effect of prior tonic work. Within one 
workout, the traccs of all the training tasks arc summed, which results in the same effect, despite these tasks being 
done in succession.
These findings should not be considered to disprove in general the appropriateness of using a complex of 
means in training, which exploits the positive after-effect of preceding strength work to enhance the training effect 
of the subsequent speed-strength and speed work. Since the experiment was conducted on a group of novice 
athletes, it is very likely that their lower level of special fitness excluded the possibility for exploiting this 
phenomenon adequately. A well-trained athlete can expect the preceding strength work to have a positive effect 
on the training effect of speed-strength and speed work in a training programme. However, the validity of this 
hypothesis can be established conclusively only by careful experimentation.
In an experiment with junior class sprinters the specific effect of short jumping exercises and the systematic 
use of combinations of these exercises was investigated. The jumping exercises involved variations of repeated 
jumps on one and two legs, as well as variations of triple and quintuple standing broad jumps and long jumping 
exercises (multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30- 100m). One group of sprinters 
executed mainly short jumps, a second group did mainly long jumping exercises and a third group did both fora

• Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises, but not before.

The experiment showed that the plyometric method produces an additional, significant increase in the level of 
explosive strength that was first attained with resistance training. This demonstrates the use of these means in 
two appropriate stages: the first stage, which improves explosive strength, and the second stage, which stabilises 
the level of special fitness. 
There was a significant increase in all the control indicators after a period of complete 
rest following the first and sccond stages. This emphasizes that rest may be used as a training means. This is not 
a paradox, because growth and maintenance processes take place predominantly during sleep and other forms of 
passive or activc rest.
Several researchers have studied the systematic use of special strength training by highly qualified athletes 
under various training conditions (Purvin, Deniskin, Khodykin). It was established that using electromuscular 
stimulation (ES) first, followed by plyometrics yielded a larger training effect than the use of these means in the 
reverse order. However, a significantly larger training effect was obtained by using them together during the same 
stage, when, for example, ES and plyomctrics are applied concurrently with heavy resistance exercises. When the 
training is not chiefly for strength, ES and plyometrics were observed to have the lowest effect during periods of

Unidirectional emphasis on qualities such as strength or endurance may be used not only in individual worko 
but also during each microcycle (Kudelin, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1980). Research has sho 
that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is 
gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle. Moreover, the effectiveness of the conjugate 
sequence system with advanced athletes is such that the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as 
much as 20%, a phenomenon referred to as the acceleration o f specific adaptation (see 5.4.2).
However, it must be noted that unidirectional loading is effective only if one uses a diverse complcx of means 
with a single primary emphasis, together with a variety of training methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov &. 
Monograov, 1977; Verkhoshansky, 1977). Furthermore, an important condition for implementing concentrated 
loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, sincc the frequent use of these means already intensifies the 
training. In this context, the loading may be considered concentrated if its volume in the month in which it is 
applied constitutes 23-25% of the general volume for the year.
The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the 
potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on 
heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill 
or speed. Since the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect, a diminished 
loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to 
supercompensate to the desired level o f preparedness. The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated 
blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 
weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without 
adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training 
effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training.
5.4 The Principal Aims of Special S trength Training
During the initial stages of training the body reacts to any stimulus with all of its survival mcchanisms and motor 
abilities. As a result of this general adaptation response, the specific training effects which enhance working 
potential are not produced. Characteristically, there is a relatively high correlation between the various motor 
abilities and the development of even those abilities which are not directly implicated. The transfer of fitness is 
very distinct here.
As sporting proficiency grows, so the adaptation response becomes more selective. Functional adaptation is 
confined primarily to those systems which are the most active and develops in those directions which art 
determined by the specific components of the training stimulus. The close connection between separate motor 
abilities tends to diminish during the stage of high sports proficiency, the rate of development o f motor abilities 
which are not the direct object of training slows down, and the transfer phenomenon is not displayed as sharply 
as before. Thus, the direction of progress is determined entirely by the specific components of the training 
stimulus. Since sport achievements at the high levels of sports proficiency are produced by a complex of specific 
motor abilities, the regime of the means used should contain an optimal combination of specific training means.
It is now appropriate to formulate a set of general principles for organising special strength training, based on 
the specific characteristics of physical training and the long-term dynamics of the STS (Sports Training Process). 
In general, they express the chief ways o f exploiting these characteristics and form the foundation of a new 
system of sport training, although they do not exclude all of the traditional principles and rules. These principles 
are:
• Converging the partial effects of strength training means
• Accelerating specific adaptation
• Specific correspondence of the training effect
• Maintaining the strength training effect.
5.4.1 Converging the Partial E ffects of Strength Training Means
The principle of converging the partial effects o f strength training means is fundamental to the long-term 
organisation of strength training. It is achieved by the convergence of all the different partial training effects, i.e. 
the gradual convergence of their cumulative training effect to those important specific characteristics which are 
essential to the functioning of the body in a particular sport.

# The Long-Term Delayed Training Effect: Volume Well Above the Optimum Depresses Speed-Strength, Then a Timed Volume Cut Lets It Rise Above Baseline

**What it is** — The authors report "a steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 weeks)" caused by "voluminous strength loading," after which "speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it" (Nikitin 1977; Mironenko 1979; Antonova 1982; Levchenko 1982). Because this "does not agree with established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness" and "is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining," it became "a subject of special study" (PDF p. 374 / printed p. 363, checked against the page image). They then state a dose-response rule: "The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body reacts with diminished response." "If the volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work-capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (same page).

Their characterisation (Fig 6.31, PDF pp. 374-375 / printed pp. 363-364, checked against the page images), points 1, 2 and 4:
1. "Concentration of strength loading is the basic condition for the beginning of the LDTE."
2. "The lower the speed-strength levels fall (within an optimal range) during the concentration of strength loading stage, the higher they rise in the subsequent LDTE phase (graphs of F1 and F2). Excessive concentration of strength loading leads to a more significant drop in speed-strength and disruption of adaptation (graph F3)." In the figure, F3 dips lowest and only creeps back toward the baseline by the end of T2; F1 and F2 end above it.
4. "A subsequent moderate volume of general developmental work, combined with special work of gradually increasing intensity contributes to eliciting the LDTE."

Points 3 (non-intensive means) and 5 (T2 about equal to T1, observed 4-12 weeks, individualised) are already quoted in [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] and [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]].

**Figures.** Fig 6.29 (sprinters, PDF p. 374, read from the image): a shaded rectangle marks the loading period from month 0 to about month 2.5; three curves (starting, explosive and absolute strength, the dips not labelled separately) fall to about 85-96% of initial, recross 100% at about month 2, and at month 4 sit at about 125% (starting), about 119% (explosive) and about 112% (absolute). Fig 6.30 (middle-distance runners, Zhdanovich 1980, PDF p. 375): during a shaded block from about month 1.3 to about month 4.3, vertical jump rises to about 7% and then falls to about 4.5% by month 8; stride length and ten standing long jumps keep rising after the block, to about 11% and about 9-9.5%. The text says vertical jump falls in the competition stage and offers a hedged reason: "One may assume that the reason for this phenomenon is the increase in volume of intense distance work" (PDF p. 374). LDTE after concentrated strength loading is also reported in swimming (Rudokene 1981) and ice-skating (Kabachkova et al 1982).

Two further points: athletes "invariably do not allow or do not have sufficient time for recuperation after extensive strength loading," which minimises the LDTE and forces the body "to unjustifiably deplete its current adaptation energy and sometimes draw upon its deep adaptation energy" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). And "one must differentiate between maintenance of the training effect and the LDTE of loading": maintenance is "the retention of functional adaptation for a given period after training has ceased"; the LDTE is "the relatively prolonged increase in the functional indicators as a result of specially organised, concentrated volumes of loading" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors say the volume-performance link is "characteristically simple" but give no physiological mechanism for the delayed rise in 6.10's strength material; they note that the "physiological conditions, mechanisms and characteristics of the LDTE until recently have not been a subject of much research" (PDF p. 374). Inference: the library holds two readings of the same curve shape, supercompensation or adaptive reconstruction ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]) and fitness-fatigue, where fatigue masks fitness until volume drops ([[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]); the book does not settle between them here.

**When to apply** — Planning a concentrated strength block for an advanced athlete when the aim is a later rise in speed-strength, accepting a planned dip during the block. Inference: a dip in speed-strength during such a block is the expected path, not by itself a signal to stop. Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the LDTE rests on one load-design move, the timed volume cut, so it fits that practice. Eric's baseline: "The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds" (line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: during a deliberate block, an mRSI drop below an athlete's usual band would be expected; the authors' own rule separates a dip "within an optimal range" from the F3 case, but gives no threshold for telling them apart.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no numbers for "optimum," "within an optimal range" or "excessive," and says the effect is individual (PDF p. 375). Figs 6.29-6.31 carry no sample sizes or statistics; Fig 6.31 is a "general scheme," not data. The 5-12 weeks on PDF p. 374 is the length of the loading stages; the 4-12 weeks on PDF p. 375 is how long the LDTE lasts. They are different quantities. Inference: in-season, when performance is needed every week, a planned multi-week dip conflicts with Eric's baseline that "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)); this is an off-season tool. The book's claim that the dip comes without "marked signs of overtraining" sits beside Bompa's framing of concentrated loading as planned overreaching ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]); Inference: that is a difference of labels, not of the observed curve.

**Example** — The authors' own: in sprinters (Fig 6.29), about 2.5 months of concentrated strength loading drove starting, explosive and absolute strength to about 85-96% of initial; by month 4 they stood at about 112-125% (values read from the image, PDF p. 374).

# Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small

**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).

**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The Addendum restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: triple jumpers whose specialised strength volume rose "by only a few percent" to "maintain" their level saw "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip, since its example fits Chapter 6, but the book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.

**Example** — The authors' own, from the Addendum (PDF p. 536, checked against the page image): triple jumpers gained speed-strength and results in May-June after concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April, then lost both quickly when they raised strength volume by a few percent to hold the gain. Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]]

# For Aerobic and Anaerobic Productivity, a Long-Term Delayed Effect Has Been Documented Only After Altitude Training

**What it is** — Under "The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work," the authors state: "With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image). Their evidence:
- **Swimmers (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974).** "significant increases" in "maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactate accumulation." "These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking place about 1 week after the altitude training. All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude."
- **Skaters (Ivanov 1977).** A 4-minute cycle-ergometer test weekly for 3 weeks at 2250 m, then for 3 weeks at sea level. At altitude, mechanical efficiency fell and oxygen consumption, energy expenditure and lactate rose; back at sea level, "the functional efficiency of the work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP" (same page).
- **Not an altitude case: swimmers under large loads (Susman 1978; no altitude is mentioned).** The authors cite this as evidence that load-induced homeostatic disturbance shows in psycho-physiological indicators, not as a documented LDTE. Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the altitude cases: hypobaric conditions gave "a very demanding training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body's homeostasis and subsequent activation of its adaptive processes" (PDF p. 376). For why the LDTE is not seen at sea level, they hedge: if it exists there, the disturbance "will occur at the level of more subtle physiological systems" not detectable by "methods used for assessing the more gross aerobic and anaerobic processes," and "adaptation apparently occurs at deeper cellular and molecular levels (e.g. in the mitochondria and endocrine system)" (Yakovlev 1957, 1974; Viru 1969, 1981; Finogenov 1979), while "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" of the central nervous and neuromuscular systems (PDF pp. 376-377). This is a stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.

**When to apply** — When planning or interpreting altitude camps: the book's one quantified case puts the peak about 1 week after a 3-week stay, with changes lasting more than 4 weeks. When judging a heavy endurance block: the authors point to psycho-physiological and neuromuscular indicators as the place a hidden disturbance may show. Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a neuromuscular marker of that kind is the sort of indicator the authors suggest, though they name reaction, precision and tracking tasks, not jump tests.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample sizes, controls or statistics for any of the three studies, and the skater study has no non-altitude comparison group in the text. The authors say plainly that the LDTE in sea-level distance training is not documented; do not carry the strength-block LDTE timings ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]) over to aerobic work. The LDTE they do report in cyclic sports (middle-distance running, swimming, skating) follows concentrated strength loading and shows in strength-endurance measures, not in aerobic productivity (PDF p. 374). Inference: altitude camps are rare in American collegiate football, so this entry matters mainly for endurance or Olympic-sport programmes.

**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers after 3 weeks at 1700 m improved immediately, peaked about 1 week after returning, and kept the gains for more than 4 weeks (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974; PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365).

# Distributed and Concentrated Loading Both Work at Medium Qualification; Highly Qualified Athletes Need Concentration

**What it is** — For loading of one primary emphasis, the authors separate "distributed loading," "a relatively uniform distribution of means during an annual cycle," from "concentrated loading," "the concentration of means over definite training stages" (PDF p. 371 / printed p. 360, checked against the page image). Their claim: "Research indicates that both methods are successful in training athletes of medium qualification. The concentrated loading method is appropriate for the training of highly qualified athletes." The evidence named: "distribution of glycolytic work over the annual cycle of highly qualified sprinters raises the loading volume, but does not increase the effectiveness of the loading. However, by concentrating the volume of glycolytic work at certain stages, the work can be executed at a smaller volume but with a more significant improvement in speed-endurance (Kornelyuk, 1980)." "Similar results" are reported for concentrated special strength work in sprinters (Levchenko 1986), middle-distance runners (Sirenko & Zhdanovich 1982), boxers (Filimonov 1979) and jumpers (Mironenko & Antonova 1981). Their conclusion, italicised in the original: "concentration of the volume of uni-directional loading produces more extensive functional changes and greater improvement in the athlete's physical fitness" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "The regular use of training with distributed loading which is dispersed over a prolonged period evokes only a transient functional reaction which does not enhance the development of long-term adaptation. Distributed loading initially can yield some rise in functional level but its training potential soon drops because of rapid adaptation of the body to the training stimuli" (PDF p. 371). No physiological mechanism beyond that is given.

**When to apply** — For advanced athletes whose progress has stalled under an even, year-round spread of one kind of work, concentrate that work into defined stages. The authors list concentration of loading over time among their four organisational principles of special strength training (PDF pp. 370-371). Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization ... waving volume week to week ... is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: undulation is about week-to-week waves and concentration is about where a quality's volume sits across the year; the two can coexist, but the book's claim is that an evenly spread quality loses its effect for advanced athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample sizes, effect sizes or design for any of the cited studies, and gives no definition here of "medium" versus "highly qualified." **Contested across the library:** the vault brief of Issurin (2016) records that he judged the evidence for Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model insufficient for broad use in high-performance combat, team-sport and swimming preparation, that the reviewed combat and team-sport studies improved fitness measures but did not report team-practice or competition outcomes, and that he placed the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], brief citing review pp. 6, 11; paraphrase, not Issurin's wording). The Supertraining evidence above comes from sprinters, middle-distance runners, boxers and jumpers, Inference: its boxing study (Filimonov 1979) is a combat-sport case Issurin's review would put in doubt. Inference: for football, where many qualities must be held at once, the claim applies to a single quality inside an otherwise mixed programme rather than to the whole plan. Eric's baseline: "incompatible qualities ... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" and "the rest are trained at a retention dose" (line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**Example** — The authors' own: highly qualified sprinters who concentrated glycolytic work into certain stages did less of it but improved speed-endurance more than when the same kind of work was spread over the year (Kornelyuk 1980; PDF p. 371 / printed p. 360). Inference: in an off-season, glycolytic conditioning could be placed in one or two short stages rather than a little every week; Eric's baseline notes that staff "do program it in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)).

# Within One Session, the Order of Paired Explosive-Strength Means Matters Less Than Their Volume and Contrast

**What it is** — For explosive strength, the authors list "brief combinations of training means" that give "a positive cumulative effect": "short and long jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises and jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises with 30% and 90% of maximum"; "barbell exercises and the plyometric method of developing explosive-strength"; "leaping with kettle-bells and jumping exercises"; "barbell exercises and leaping with kettle-bells" (PDF p. 371 / printed p. 360, checked against the page image). Then: "In a single training session the order of the above means, combined in a systematic complex is fairly unimportant, since the length of time for which the body maintains the after-effect of training stress exceeds the duration of the workout." In italics: "concerning the development of explosive strength, the order of the means is not fundamentally as important as the volume of the loading and the degree of contrast between the different training means." Yet in the next sentence: "Nevertheless, one should still preserve the above order of combining means in each case, since this provides the favourable effect of a brief rise in fitness state, which the first exercise produces as the second one is executed (see Ch 5.3)." Their delivery rule: "employ them sequentially with active rest between each series," and when repeating a series, "vary the exercises to avoid monotony and to maintain the optimal rest interval" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "During this session and the subsequent restoration period, a generalised summation of the after-effects of the entire complex of training influences of different primary emphasis occurs, which produces the same cumulative effect, generally regardless of their sequence" (PDF p. 371). They add that "it is still sensible to apply the recommended scheme of Figure 1.7 to minimise the risk of reducing skill and safety." Figure 1.7 in this edition is a torque diagram in 1.2 (PDF pp. 28-29, text layer). Inference: that cross-reference appears to be wrong and the intended scheme is unclear.

**When to apply** — Building a contrast or complex session for explosive strength from one of the listed pairs: settle the volume and the contrast between the two means first, then keep the listed order as a secondary choice. Inference: when equipment or space forces the order to flip on a given day, the authors' text says little is lost within the session. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

15	# The Long-Term Delayed Training Effect: Volume Well Above the Optimum Depresses Speed-Strength, Then a Timed Volume Cut Lets It Rise Above Baseline
16	
17	**What it is** — The authors report "a steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 weeks)" caused by "voluminous strength loading," after which "speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it" (Nikitin 1977; Mironenko 1979; Antonova 1982; Levchenko 1982). Because this "does not agree with established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness" and "is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining," it became "a subject of special study" (PDF p. 374 / printed p. 363, checked against the page image). They then state a dose-response rule: "The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body reacts with diminished response." "If the volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work-capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (same page).
18	
19	Their characterisation (Fig 6.31, PDF pp. 374-375 / printed pp. 363-364, checked against the page images), points 1, 2 and 4:
20	1. "Concentration of strength loading is the basic condition for the beginning of the LDTE."
21	2. "The lower the speed-strength levels fall (within an optimal range) during the concentration of strength loading stage, the higher they rise in the subsequent LDTE phase (graphs of F1 and F2). Excessive concentration of strength loading leads to a more significant drop in speed-strength and disruption of adaptation (graph F3)." In the figure, F3 dips lowest and only creeps back toward the baseline by the end of T2; F1 and F2 end above it.
22	4. "A subsequent moderate volume of general developmental work, combined with special work of gradually increasing intensity contributes to eliciting the LDTE."
23	
24	Points 3 (non-intensive means) and 5 (T2 about equal to T1, observed 4-12 weeks, individualised) are already quoted in [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] and [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]].
25	
26	**Figures.** Fig 6.29 (sprinters, PDF p. 374, read from the image): a shaded rectangle marks the loading period from month 0 to about month 2.5; three curves (starting, explosive and absolute strength, the dips not labelled separately) fall to about 85-96% of initial, recross 100% at about month 2, and at month 4 sit at about 125% (starting), about 119% (explosive) and about 112% (absolute). Fig 6.30 (middle-distance runners, Zhdanovich 1980, PDF p. 375): during a shaded block from about month 1.3 to about month 4.3, vertical jump rises to about 7% and then falls to about 4.5% by month 8; stride length and ten standing long jumps keep rising after the block, to about 11% and about 9-9.5%. The text says vertical jump falls in the competition stage and offers a hedged reason: "One may assume that the reason for this phenomenon is the increase in volume of intense distance work" (PDF p. 374). LDTE after concentrated strength loading is also reported in swimming (Rudokene 1981) and ice-skating (Kabachkova et al 1982).
27	
28	Two further points: athletes "invariably do not allow or do not have sufficient time for recuperation after extensive strength loading," which minimises the LDTE and forces the body "to unjustifiably deplete its current adaptation energy and sometimes draw upon its deep adaptation energy" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364). And "one must differentiate between maintenance of the training effect and the LDTE of loading": maintenance is "the retention of functional adaptation for a given period after training has ceased"; the LDTE is "the relatively prolonged increase in the functional indicators as a result of specially organised, concentrated volumes of loading" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).
29	
30	**Why it works** — The authors say the volume-performance link is "characteristically simple" but give no physiological mechanism for the delayed rise in 6.10's strength material; they note that the "physiological conditions, mechanisms and characteristics of the LDTE until recently have not been a subject of much research" (PDF p. 374). Inference: the library holds two readings of the same curve shape, supercompensation or adaptive reconstruction ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]) and fitness-fatigue, where fatigue masks fitness until volume drops ([[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]]); the book does not settle between them here.
31	
32	**When to apply** — Planning a concentrated strength block for an advanced athlete when the aim is a later rise in speed-strength, accepting a planned dip during the block. Inference: a dip in speed-strength during such a block is the expected path, not by itself a signal to stop. Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the LDTE rests on one load-design move, the timed volume cut, so it fits that practice. Eric's baseline: "The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds" (line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: during a deliberate block, an mRSI drop below an athlete's usual band would be expected; the authors' own rule separates a dip "within an optimal range" from the F3 case, but gives no threshold for telling them apart.
33	
34	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no numbers for "optimum," "within an optimal range" or "excessive," and says the effect is individual (PDF p. 375). Figs 6.29-6.31 carry no sample sizes or statistics; Fig 6.31 is a "general scheme," not data. The 5-12 weeks on PDF p. 374 is the length of the loading stages; the 4-12 weeks on PDF p. 375 is how long the LDTE lasts. They are different quantities. Inference: in-season, when performance is needed every week, a planned multi-week dip conflicts with Eric's baseline that "in football you want to peak every Saturday" (line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)); this is an off-season tool. The book's claim that the dip comes without "marked signs of overtraining" sits beside Bompa's framing of concentrated loading as planned overreaching ([[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]); Inference: that is a difference of labels, not of the observed curve.
35	
36	**Example** — The authors' own: in sprinters (Fig 6.29), about 2.5 months of concentrated strength loading drove starting, explosive and absolute strength to about 85-96% of initial; by month 4 they stood at about 112-125% (values read from the image, PDF p. 374).
37

53	# Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small
54	
55	**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
56	1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
57	2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
58	3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).
59	
60	The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).
61	
62	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).
63	
64	**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.
65	
66	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** The Addendum restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: triple jumpers whose specialised strength volume rose "by only a few percent" to "maintain" their level saw "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip, since its example fits Chapter 6, but the book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.
67	
68	**Example** — The authors' own, from the Addendum (PDF p. 536, checked against the page image): triple jumpers gained speed-strength and results in May-June after concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April, then lost both quickly when they raised strength volume by a few percent to hold the gain. Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.
69	
70	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]]

85	# For Aerobic and Anaerobic Productivity, a Long-Term Delayed Effect Has Been Documented Only After Altitude Training
86	
87	**What it is** — Under "The Delayed Training Effect and Long Duration Work," the authors state: "With respect to aerobic and anaerobic productivity, there is no experimental data that clearly documents occurrence of the LDTE phenomenon in cyclic distance training. The exceptions are cases of intense training under the lowered oxygen conditions of high altitude" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image). Their evidence:
88	- **Swimmers (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974).** "significant increases" in "maximum aerobic capacity, the total volume of work which can be executed at the critical level of power, VO2 max and the onset of blood lactate accumulation." "These changes persisted for more than 4 weeks after 3 weeks of training at an altitude of 1700m above sea level, with a peak response taking place about 1 week after the altitude training. All of the athletes in the study improved their results immediately after training at altitude."
89	- **Skaters (Ivanov 1977).** A 4-minute cycle-ergometer test weekly for 3 weeks at 2250 m, then for 3 weeks at sea level. At altitude, mechanical efficiency fell and oxygen consumption, energy expenditure and lactate rose; back at sea level, "the functional efficiency of the work exceeded the pre-experimental levels as a result of more economical metabolism and a significantly diminished amount of anaerobically produced ATP" (same page).
90	- **Not an altitude case: swimmers under large loads (Susman 1978; no altitude is mentioned).** The authors cite this as evidence that load-induced homeostatic disturbance shows in psycho-physiological indicators, not as a documented LDTE. Large loads slowed "complex motor reactions," reduced precision of movement patterns and of "tracking a moving object," and lowered work capacity, ECG-assessed cardiovascular state, muscle tonus and adrenal-cortex hormone levels. After loads were reduced and intensity altered, these indicators rose "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image).
91	
92	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for the altitude cases: hypobaric conditions gave "a very demanding training influence which provoked persistent disturbance of the body's homeostasis and subsequent activation of its adaptive processes" (PDF p. 376). For why the LDTE is not seen at sea level, they hedge: if it exists there, the disturbance "will occur at the level of more subtle physiological systems" not detectable by "methods used for assessing the more gross aerobic and anaerobic processes," and "adaptation apparently occurs at deeper cellular and molecular levels (e.g. in the mitochondria and endocrine system)" (Yakovlev 1957, 1974; Viru 1969, 1981; Finogenov 1979), while "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators" of the central nervous and neuromuscular systems (PDF pp. 376-377). This is a stated hypothesis, not a demonstrated mechanism.
93	
94	**When to apply** — When planning or interpreting altitude camps: the book's one quantified case puts the peak about 1 week after a 3-week stay, with changes lasting more than 4 weeks. When judging a heavy endurance block: the authors point to psycho-physiological and neuromuscular indicators as the place a hidden disturbance may show. Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a neuromuscular marker of that kind is the sort of indicator the authors suggest, though they name reaction, precision and tracking tasks, not jump tests.
95	
96	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no sample sizes, controls or statistics for any of the three studies, and the skater study has no non-altitude comparison group in the text. The authors say plainly that the LDTE in sea-level distance training is not documented; do not carry the strength-block LDTE timings ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]) over to aerobic work. The LDTE they do report in cyclic sports (middle-distance running, swimming, skating) follows concentrated strength loading and shows in strength-endurance measures, not in aerobic productivity (PDF p. 374). Inference: altitude camps are rare in American collegiate football, so this entry matters mainly for endurance or Olympic-sport programmes.
97	
98	**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers after 3 weeks at 1700 m improved immediately, peaked about 1 week after returning, and kept the gains for more than 4 weeks (Vaitsekhovsky et al 1974; PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365).
99
