# Over a Year, Speed-Strength Moves Randomly at Medium Qualification, Follows the Plan in Developing Athletes, and Defies the Plan in the Highly Qualified

**What it is** — The authors say "there is very little research concerning the dynamics of the athlete's state over the annual cycle," and that "Research assessing the athlete's state 3 to 4 times a year is not very informative, since the most interesting changes in state occur between each of these stages." Laboratory studies of untrained subjects over 3-4 months (Pollock 1973) are "of little use in programming the training of highly qualified athletes." "Therefore, Verkhoshansky and his colleagues undertook research ... under the natural conditions of training athletes of various levels of qualification, recording functional indicators twice a month and correlating all changes with calculations of the training loads and volumes" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image; the third-person naming marks this framing as Siff's). The findings, for "sports requiring explosive force" (PDF pp. 377-378, checked against the page images):
- **Medium qualification.** "random increases in speed-strength ... together with insignificant changes in speed-strength during the annual cycle," fluctuations that "often do not conform to the periodisation schemes of training or the competition calendar." The stated cause: "complex training (i.e. the concurrent use of loading regimes of different primary emphasis) and the monotonous monthly distribution of the general volume of loading."
- **Non-elite athletes as proficiency grows.** "a trend towards regularity which reflects the type of training periodisation": in a monocycle (e.g. decathlon) special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations"; in a bi-cycle, "two large waves" ending in the winter and summer competitions.
- **Highly qualified athletes.** Dynamics "cannot be regulated in such a manner." "Large fluctuations in speed-strength preparedness can be of different duration and magnitude, can occur at different stages of the annual cycle and often show neither a logical correlation with traditional periodisation of training (for the given sport) nor the competition calendar."

**Why it works** — For the medium-qualification pattern the authors give the cause quoted above (complex training plus a monotonous monthly volume). For the highly qualified pattern they give no cause in this passage; the next paragraph points to unequal loading of different muscle groups as one source ([[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]]).

**When to apply** — Choosing a testing cadence and reading the results. Inference: by this passage, testing 3-4 times a year misses the changes that matter, and twice a month was the authors' working cadence. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "There is no common testing cadence across sports; each sport keeps its own schedule" (line 60, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)). Inference: the authors' twice-monthly figure is a floor a sport-by-sport schedule could be checked against. For a medium-level squad with flat, random-looking results, the authors' diagnosis points to concurrent mixed loading with an even monthly volume.

**When NOT to apply** — No sample sizes, sports or data plots are given in this section; the results are said to appear "throughout Chapter 5 and this chapter." For highly qualified athletes the passage describes irregularity without offering a rule to control it, while the same section concludes that annual dynamics "are controllable" (PDF p. 378); Inference: the two are reconciled only if control comes from the content and organisation of loading rather than from periodisation labels, which is the authors' wider argument. The categories "medium qualification," "non-elite" and "highly qualified" are Soviet classification levels and do not map cleanly onto college rosters.

**Example** — The authors' own: under monocyclic periodisation in the decathlon, special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations throughout the year," while bi-cyclic plans show two waves ending in the winter and summer competitions (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366).

# Triple Jumpers: Jumps Plus Barbell Work Depress the Plantarflexors While the Thigh Extensors Read High

**What it is** — Observing annual dynamics, the authors report that "the speed-strength of thigh extension, knee extension and plantarflexion can show different trends of change at certain training stages" (italics in the original), with "the dynamics of the explosive strength of triple jumpers" as the example (Verkhoshansky 1988; PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image). "The concurrent use of jumping and barbell exercises exerts a more intense local influence on the plantarflexors than other muscles of the lower extremity and, consequently, depresses their functional state. However, the loading is not as intense on the thigh extensors, so that their functional indicators reflect a high value. In this case, the athlete notices that movement coordination is difficult although, on the whole, he feels perfectly fit." Their prescription: when means are chosen without regard to "the differences in their primary emphasis on the specific muscle groups," the muscles' state may not match the sport's needs, harming "technical preparation" and "preparedness for competition," so "it is necessary to regulate the emphasis of the loading on the plantarflexors, and periodically decrease the loading on them, especially during the technical and immediate pre-competition training stages" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is unequal local load: the jump-plus-barbell combination hits the plantarflexors harder than the thigh extensors (PDF p. 378). They give no data on the size or timing of the difference and no physiological mechanism beyond that.

**When to apply** — When an athlete reports that coordination feels off while overall fitness feels fine, or when a whole-leg test looks normal but jumping technique is deteriorating. Eric's baseline: daily CMJ mRSI is the department's readiness marker (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: the plateau figures come largely from track-and-field and endurance athletes; for football, where qualities are trained together, the decathlete case (explosive strength rising for up to 10 months when it is not the sole aim) may be the closer analogue.
37	
38	**Example** — The authors' own contrast: explosive strength trained exclusively plateaus within 3-4 months, while in decathletes on a mono-cycle, where it is one quality among many, it can keep rising for up to 10 months (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359).

44	=================== principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue.md
45	# Volume Drives Long-Term Adaptation and Prepares Connective Tissue; Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work
46	
47	**What it is** — The authors give volume two roles. First: "The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes of loading (within optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity" (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358, checked against the page image). Second, in sports with "brief, highly concentrated efforts": "the mechanical integrity of the ligamentous-joint apparatus can become the limiting factor to the progress of sporting performance" (italics in the original). "If these connective tissues are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping" (same page).
48	
49	Volume alone is not enough: "the influence of the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its duration and intensity" (PDF p. 369). Magnitude is set "first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification": the higher the qualification, the larger the yearly and stage volume, and the share of "specialised loading" grows (Panov 1975; Zhikharevich 1976; Vankov 1977; Matveyev 1977; Gilyazova 1978). The annual volume is "established individually" from the preceding stages; "A more serious task" is the optimal volume per month, stage or phase (same page). On intensity: it "determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body," regulates "the training potential of the given means," frequency and intervals, and "the ratio of the volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage," a measure of "loading concentration relative to time." "Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1)" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image).
50	
51	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one quoted: prolonged homeostatic disturbance mobilises "energy resources and plastic reserves" and moves the body from an acute to a general, then long-term, adaptive reaction (PDF p. 369). For connective tissue they refer back to 1.6 and 1.7.2 and give no further mechanism here.
52	
53	**When to apply** — Building a multi-year plan (raise annual volume, within limits, as qualification rises) and opening each year with extensive moderate-intensity work before intensifying, especially in jumping and other high-impact events. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill ...)" (line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' "extensive low intensity loading" before intensification is close to the work-capacity base of that hierarchy.
54	
55	**When NOT to apply** — "within optimal limits" is not quantified, and the rule to raise volume every year cannot run indefinitely; the authors elsewhere set a limit by current adaptation reserves (PDF p. 370) and an optimum above which the LDTE pattern appears (PDF p. 374, [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]). The joint-injury link is stated as frequent in four sports with no data. Inference: in American collegiate football, where many athletes are four- or five-year players, a rising-volume rule would need to be weighed against Eric's baseline that recovery is handled "through training-load design alone" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)), since nothing else would catch an overshoot. The book's 4.1.2 passage gives volume two different functions (a functional base and endurance development; [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]]); Inference: the two lists overlap on the "base" role and differ on the second, so read them together rather than as rival definitions.
56	
57	**Example** — The authors' own: gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping, where joint injury "occurs frequently" if connective tissue has not been prepared by extensive moderate-intensity work before peak dynamic loads (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358). Inference: a jumper's year would open with weeks of moderate-volume, lower-impact jumping and strength work before depth jumps.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]], [[framework--logical-scheme-of-training-management-load-fitness-state-external-interactions]] (6.4, training potential as relative to current fitness), [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]

63	=================== framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state.md
64	# Three Levels of Change in Fitness State: Long-Term (Volume), Medium-Term (Content), Short-Term (Acute and Largely Random)
65	
66	**What it is** — From Sirenko's study and "other studies of the influence of training loads on functional indicators," the authors identify "three levels of change in an athlete's fitness state during training" (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image):
67	1. "A long-term level characterised by the steady rise in the athlete's special work-capacity," over "one or more years," based on "long-term adaptation, promoted chiefly by the volume of loading."
68	2. "A medium-term level characterised by less stable and readily reversible functional changes, the basis for which is compensatory adaptation," over "lengthy training stages of up to 5-6 months," produced with volume by "the characteristics of its contents, in particular, the proportion of intensive means in the total volume of loading."
69	3. "A short-term level characterised by brief, but not precisely measurable, changes in the functional indicators," the "acute reaction to the training load" within the microcycle, elicited by "the magnitude of the load, the intensity of loading, the individual ability of the athlete to endure the loading and his restorative capabilities." "At this level, the dynamics of the functional indicators are largely random and at times unpredictable. This level is not determined by the adaptation of the first two levels and is important only for organisation of the microcycle and achievement of the immediate effect of the current loading."
70	
71	Their conclusion: "the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state during the annual cycle are controllable," so training should be built "by first of all taking into account the dynamics of the athlete's special physical preparedness (SPP)" (PDF p. 378). "The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time"; "Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, text layer; page image not opened).
72	
73	**Why it works** — The authors say the dependence of fitness on load "is determined by definite adaptive processes" and name the basis of each level (long-term adaptation, compensatory adaptation, acute reaction). They do not explain why the short-term level is independent of the other two.
74	
75	**When to apply** — Deciding which signal to act on: microcycle-level swings guide the week's organisation only; stage-level trends reflect the content and share of intensive means; year-on-year trends reflect volume. Eric's baseline: "Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 64, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: that split maps onto the authors' levels 1-2 versus level 3. Eric's baseline: daily jumps "build the rolling baseline and SWC; Wednesday is the single decision read that changes the week" (line 255, Tension 12 status, resolved 2026-10-02 by Eric). Inference: using a rolling baseline and SWC is one way to separate the "largely random" short-term level from a real trend.
76	
77	**When NOT to apply** — The time spans (one or more years, up to 5-6 months, microcycle) are given without data. The claim that timing a peak is "not especially complex" is cited to unnamed research ("Research shows"), with no study named. Inference: calling short-term changes "not precisely measurable" reflects the authors' tools; it does not by itself mean modern daily testing carries no signal, though the authors would limit its use to microcycle decisions.
78	
79	**Example** — The authors' own anchor: Sirenko's (1980) middle-distance runners, where the same running volume with a different distribution of strength means changed the stage-level and competition results ([[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]]; PDF p. 378). Inference: a drop in one Wednesday mRSI read after a heavy Monday is level-3 noise unless it persists across reads; a decline across a six-week stage points to the stage's content.
80	
81	**Related** — [[claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification]], [[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]], [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]]

85	=================== claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification.md
86	# Over a Year, Speed-Strength Moves Randomly at Medium Qualification, Follows the Plan in Developing Athletes, and Defies the Plan in the Highly Qualified
87	
88	**What it is** — The authors say "there is very little research concerning the dynamics of the athlete's state over the annual cycle," and that "Research assessing the athlete's state 3 to 4 times a year is not very informative, since the most interesting changes in state occur between each of these stages." Laboratory studies of untrained subjects over 3-4 months (Pollock 1973) are "of little use in programming the training of highly qualified athletes." "Therefore, Verkhoshansky and his colleagues undertook research ... under the natural conditions of training athletes of various levels of qualification, recording functional indicators twice a month and correlating all changes with calculations of the training loads and volumes" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image; the third-person naming marks this framing as Siff's). The findings, for "sports requiring explosive force" (PDF pp. 377-378, checked against the page images):
89	- **Medium qualification.** "random increases in speed-strength ... together with insignificant changes in speed-strength during the annual cycle," fluctuations that "often do not conform to the periodisation schemes of training or the competition calendar." The stated cause: "complex training (i.e. the concurrent use of loading regimes of different primary emphasis) and the monotonous monthly distribution of the general volume of loading."
90	- **Non-elite athletes as proficiency grows.** "a trend towards regularity which reflects the type of training periodisation": in a monocycle (e.g. decathlon) special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations"; in a bi-cycle, "two large waves" ending in the winter and summer competitions.
91	- **Highly qualified athletes.** Dynamics "cannot be regulated in such a manner." "Large fluctuations in speed-strength preparedness can be of different duration and magnitude, can occur at different stages of the annual cycle and often show neither a logical correlation with traditional periodisation of training (for the given sport) nor the competition calendar."
92	
93	**Why it works** — For the medium-qualification pattern the authors give the cause quoted above (complex training plus a monotonous monthly volume). For the highly qualified pattern they give no cause in this passage; the next paragraph points to unequal loading of different muscle groups as one source ([[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]]).
94	
95	**When to apply** — Choosing a testing cadence and reading the results. Inference: by this passage, testing 3-4 times a year misses the changes that matter, and twice a month was the authors' working cadence. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "There is no common testing cadence across sports; each sport keeps its own schedule" (line 60, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)). Inference: the authors' twice-monthly figure is a floor a sport-by-sport schedule could be checked against. For a medium-level squad with flat, random-looking results, the authors' diagnosis points to concurrent mixed loading with an even monthly volume.
96	
97	**When NOT to apply** — No sample sizes, sports or data plots are given in this section; the results are said to appear "throughout Chapter 5 and this chapter." For highly qualified athletes the passage describes irregularity without offering a rule to control it, while the same section concludes that annual dynamics "are controllable" (PDF p. 378); Inference: the two are reconciled only if control comes from the content and organisation of loading rather than from periodisation labels, which is the authors' wider argument. The categories "medium qualification," "non-elite" and "highly qualified" are Soviet classification levels and do not map cleanly onto college rosters.
98	
99	**Example** — The authors' own: under monocyclic periodisation in the decathlon, special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations throughout the year," while bi-cyclic plans show two waves ending in the winter and summer competitions (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366).
100	
101	**Related** — [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]], [[claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]

105	=================== case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high.md
106	# Triple Jumpers: Jumps Plus Barbell Work Depress the Plantarflexors While the Thigh Extensors Read High
107	
108	**What it is** — Observing annual dynamics, the authors report that "the speed-strength of thigh extension, knee extension and plantarflexion can show different trends of change at certain training stages" (italics in the original), with "the dynamics of the explosive strength of triple jumpers" as the example (Verkhoshansky 1988; PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image). "The concurrent use of jumping and barbell exercises exerts a more intense local influence on the plantarflexors than other muscles of the lower extremity and, consequently, depresses their functional state. However, the loading is not as intense on the thigh extensors, so that their functional indicators reflect a high value. In this case, the athlete notices that movement coordination is difficult although, on the whole, he feels perfectly fit." Their prescription: when means are chosen without regard to "the differences in their primary emphasis on the specific muscle groups," the muscles' state may not match the sport's needs, harming "technical preparation" and "preparedness for competition," so "it is necessary to regulate the emphasis of the loading on the plantarflexors, and periodically decrease the loading on them, especially during the technical and immediate pre-competition training stages" (same page).
109	
110	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is unequal local load: the jump-plus-barbell combination hits the plantarflexors harder than the thigh extensors (PDF p. 378). They give no data on the size or timing of the difference and no physiological mechanism beyond that.
111	
112	**When to apply** — When an athlete reports that coordination feels off while overall fitness feels fine, or when a whole-leg test looks normal but jumping technique is deteriorating. Eric's baseline: daily CMJ mRSI is the department's readiness marker (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a two-leg CMJ is driven heavily by the hip and knee extensors, so by this case a depressed plantarflexor state could hide behind a normal CMJ; a calf-specific test would be the place to look. Eric's baseline: "The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks 'Mid-Thigh Pull' setting" (line 78, Inferred (protocol)). Inference: that existing test could check this case, though the book does not mention isometric testing for it.
113	
114	**When NOT to apply** — One cited observation in one event, with no numbers shown in the text; treat it as a hypothesis. Inference: whether a CMJ would miss the plantarflexor drop is untested here; the book does not discuss jump tests in this passage.
115	
116	**Example** — The authors' own: triple jumpers doing concurrent jumping and barbell work, whose plantarflexors were depressed while thigh-extensor indicators read high, and who reported difficult coordination while feeling fit; the fix was to cut plantarflexor loading periodically, above all in technical and pre-competition stages (PDF p. 378).
117	
118	**Related** — [[claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification]], [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]] (plantarflexor strength as an outcome), [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]

=================== framework--three-viewpoints-on-organising-endurance-development.md
# Three Viewpoints on Building Endurance Across the Year: Concurrent, Sequential, and Concurrent With a Shifting Emphasis

**What it is** — The authors first set two conditions that make endurance sequencing "more complex" than explosive-strength sequencing: in cyclic sports "the fundamental sport activity is traditionally the chief means of developing special endurance," so development "depends on the optimal selection of the relative volumes of work of different intensity and duration"; and "Endurance training causes more profound changes than explosive training within the body and requires more time for restoration," which pushes toward concurrent means "which may not always be appropriate for highly qualified athletes (Platonov, 1980)" (PDF p. 373 / printed p. 362, checked against the page image). They then describe "two opposing viewpoints" and a third (same page):
1. **Concurrent.** "concurrent development of general and special endurance" (Matveyev 1970; Ogoltsov 1971; Nabatnikova 1972), introducing "special endurance loading right from the beginning of the preparatory period." Corroborated "with athletes who had not yet reached the highest levels of sports mastery," namely junior middle-distance runners (Baranov 1969), swimmers (Kuzovenkov 1969) and skiers (Malikov 1974).
2. **Sequential.** "one begins by enhancing cardiovascular capability, followed by anaerobic-glycolytic endurance, and finally, short-term endurance (the creatine phosphate process)." "The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-effect of anaerobic work" (Ozolin 1959, 1970; Volkov 1963; Yakovlev 1957; Borisov 1979; Loktev 1978). "When one's cardiovascular ability is insufficient, an excessive increase in the volume of anaerobic means causes a decrease in sporting performance" (Naumenko 1978; Vavilov 1977; Serafimova 1974; Morzhevikov 1980).
3. **Third viewpoint.** "the increase in volume of concurrent aerobic and anaerobic training means, but with a sequential change in emphasis from general to special endurance," shown effective "for highly qualified middle-distance runners (Doroshchenko, 1976; Loktev, 1978; Borisov, 1979), as well as for multi-year training (Linyets, 1979)." The authors hedge: "One can assume that this system represents a compromise which combines the benefits of concurrent and sequential special endurance training."

**Why it works** — For viewpoint 2 the authors give a mechanism: "A gradual increase in the duration of cardiovascular loading leads to an accumulation of energy substrates and an increase in the body's energy potential (Yakovlev, et al, 1960)," and "Here, the intensity of loading, rather than its volume is of principal significance (Astrand & Rodahl, 1970)" (PDF p. 373). For viewpoints 1 and 3 they give the planners' assumptions, not mechanisms.

**When to apply** — Choosing how to order general and special endurance across a preparatory period. Inference: by the populations named, viewpoint 1 is the documented choice for athletes below the top level, and viewpoint 3 for highly qualified middle-distance runners; viewpoint 2 carries the warning about adding anaerobic volume before the aerobic base is adequate. Eric's baseline: aerobic work is kept "below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit). Eric's baseline: glycolytic conditioning is programmed "in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)). Inference: placing that glycolytic work after an aerobic base fits viewpoint 2's warning.

**When NOT to apply** — These are endurance-sport findings (running, swimming, skiing); the book gives no sample sizes or effect sizes, and the third viewpoint's superiority is an assumption ("One can assume"). Internal note: the "intensity ... rather than its volume" remark sits beside 6.9.4's emphasis on volume as the driver of long-term adaptation ([[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]]); Inference: the remark is scoped to cardiovascular loading in viewpoint 2, so this is a difference of scope rather than a contradiction. The 6.9.4 sentence that anaerobic volume helps "only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work" (PDF p. 370) reads against viewpoint 2's aerobic-first order; see [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], where that wording is flagged as unclear. Inference: for football, where the energy-system priorities differ from middle-distance running (baseline line 116), these models are background, not a template.

**Example** — The authors' own population for viewpoint 3: highly qualified middle-distance runners whose aerobic and anaerobic volume rose together while the emphasis shifted from general to special endurance over the annual cycle (Doroshchenko 1976; Loktev 1978; Borisov 1979; PDF p. 373). No numbers are given.

**Related** — [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]] (5.3, the same Ozolin-Volkov-Yakovlev-Borisov sequence), [[framework--positive-and-negative-sequences-of-endurance-loading]], [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]

=================== claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality.md
# How Long One Emphasis Keeps Paying: Explosive Strength Plateaus in 3-4 Months, Aerobic Fitness in 2-3, Glycolytic Capacity Peaks at About 4

**What it is** — The authors say the duration of a load "can easily be miscalculated by the average coach," and that besides the overall limit set by the body's current adaptation reserves, "there is also an upper limit to the duration of using any specialised training means with a primary emphasis, the exceeding of which is detrimental to the development of maximum and explosive strength, as well as to the growth of aerobic and anaerobic capacity. Exceeding this limit does not enhance fitness and wastes the athlete's time and energy" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image). They admit "there is no special research directed at determining the optimal length of time," and offer "indirect data" (same page):
- **Absolute strength.** A "linear increase ... which slows down as the limit of this optimal time-span of training is reached"; yet in highly qualified athletes "absolute strength increases with little variation, rising continuously during the year's training."
- **Explosive strength.** "the sharper its growth, the earlier it plateaus. When one is emphasizing the development of explosive strength exclusively, the plateau appears within 3-4 months." Where it "is not the key ability (e.g. in a mono-cycle of periodisation in the annual training of decathletes)," it "can continue (with some fluctuation) for up to 10 months."
- **Aerobic.** "significant increases in aerobic efficiency even within one month" (Borisov 1979; Sirenko 1980). Aerobic fitness and aerobic-zone loading "(at a HR of 120-170 beats/minute)" rise together, "linear over a 2-3 months period"; after that, "Despite increased loading volume, the aerobic fitness indicators do not increase significantly ... but fluctuate around the maximum level achieved" (five citations, Zatsiorsky et al 1974 to Sirenko 1980).
- **Anaerobic-glycolytic.** "About 4 months are necessary to achieve the highest results in anaerobic-glycolytic productivity" (four citations). Then: "Increasing the volume of anaerobic work produces a positive effect only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work, thereby stimulating the aerobic reaction (Serafimova, 1974; Naumenko, 1978)."

The scope note: the figures apply to "the natural conditions of an athlete's preparation," with other tasks trained alongside, match the volumes "highly qualified athletes use," and are "not definitive. However, they offer a preliminary guide" (PDF p. 370).

**Why it works** — The authors tie the slowing of gains to "exhaustion of the body's current adaptation energy (see 1.16)" (PDF p. 370). No further mechanism is given per quality.

**When to apply** — Setting the length of a stage that emphasises one quality, and deciding when a plateau means "change the stimulus" rather than "add volume." Inference: an aerobic emphasis that has run 2-3 months without further gain is, by these figures, at its ceiling for now, and more volume is not the lever. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: these time limits give a rough expectation of when a plateau is due.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors call the data indirect and the durations provisional. **Unclear wording:** the anaerobic sentence says anaerobic volume helps "only if it precedes a significant volume of aerobic work" (PDF p. 370), but on PDF p. 373 the sequential model puts aerobic first ("The introduction of aerobic work in this sequence promotes the training-effect of anaerobic work") and on PDF p. 372 "glycolytic-anaerobic exercises follow large volumes of aerobic work" is listed as a negative interaction. Inference: the p. 370 sentence may mean "is preceded by," which would fit p. 373 but not the session-level warning on p. 372; the book does not resolve it. These are times to plateau under one emphasis; they are not residual (detraining) durations, which Issurin gives separately ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]). Inference: the plateau figures come largely from track-and-field and endurance athletes; for football, where qualities are trained together, the decathlete case (explosive strength rising for up to 10 months when it is not the sole aim) may be the closer analogue.

**Example** — The authors' own contrast: explosive strength trained exclusively plateaus within 3-4 months, while in decathletes on a mono-cycle, where it is one quality among many, it can keep rising for up to 10 months (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359).

**Related** — [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive]], [[framework--three-viewpoints-on-organising-endurance-development]], [[framework--positive-and-negative-sequences-of-endurance-loading]], [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]], [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/principle--accommodation-and-the-diminishing-returns-law]]

=================== principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue.md
# Volume Drives Long-Term Adaptation and Prepares Connective Tissue; Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work

**What it is** — The authors give volume two roles. First: "The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes of loading (within optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity" (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358, checked against the page image). Second, in sports with "brief, highly concentrated efforts": "the mechanical integrity of the ligamentous-joint apparatus can become the limiting factor to the progress of sporting performance" (italics in the original). "If these connective tissues are not prepared by extensive work of moderate intensity, then the great dynamic overloading encountered at the level of peak performance can lead to severe joint injury. This occurs frequently in gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping" (same page).

Volume alone is not enough: "the influence of the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its duration and intensity" (PDF p. 369). Magnitude is set "first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification": the higher the qualification, the larger the yearly and stage volume, and the share of "specialised loading" grows (Panov 1975; Zhikharevich 1976; Vankov 1977; Matveyev 1977; Gilyazova 1978). The annual volume is "established individually" from the preceding stages; "A more serious task" is the optimal volume per month, stage or phase (same page). On intensity: it "determines the strength and specificity of its effect on the body," regulates "the training potential of the given means," frequency and intervals, and "the ratio of the volume of the loading divided by the time taken to reach the maximum load in a given stage," a measure of "loading concentration relative to time." "Intensification of loading is permitted during specific stages in the annual cycle and only after preliminary preparation with extensive low intensity loading (see Fig 6.1)" (PDF p. 370 / printed p. 359, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is the one quoted: prolonged homeostatic disturbance mobilises "energy resources and plastic reserves" and moves the body from an acute to a general, then long-term, adaptive reaction (PDF p. 369). For connective tissue they refer back to 1.6 and 1.7.2 and give no further mechanism here.

**When to apply** — Building a multi-year plan (raise annual volume, within limits, as qualification rises) and opening each year with extensive moderate-intensity work before intensifying, especially in jumping and other high-impact events. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill ...)" (line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' "extensive low intensity loading" before intensification is close to the work-capacity base of that hierarchy.

**When NOT to apply** — "within optimal limits" is not quantified, and the rule to raise volume every year cannot run indefinitely; the authors elsewhere set a limit by current adaptation reserves (PDF p. 370) and an optimum above which the LDTE pattern appears (PDF p. 374, [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]). The joint-injury link is stated as frequent in four sports with no data. Inference: in American collegiate football, where many athletes are four- or five-year players, a rising-volume rule would need to be weighed against Eric's baseline that recovery is handled "through training-load design alone" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)), since nothing else would catch an overshoot. The book's 4.1.2 passage gives volume two different functions (a functional base and endurance development; [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]]); Inference: the two lists overlap on the "base" role and differ on the second, so read them together rather than as rival definitions.

**Example** — The authors' own: gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping, where joint injury "occurs frequently" if connective tissue has not been prepared by extensive moderate-intensity work before peak dynamic loads (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358). Inference: a jumper's year would open with weeks of moderate-volume, lower-impact jumping and strength work before depth jumps.

**Related** — [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[heuristic--structured-load-progression-beats-volume-alone-or-random-combination]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[heuristic--preparatory-progression-before-depth-jumps]], [[framework--logical-scheme-of-training-management-load-fitness-state-external-interactions]] (6.4, training potential as relative to current fitness), [[heuristic--replace-means-as-their-training-effect-fades]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]

=================== framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state.md
# Three Levels of Change in Fitness State: Long-Term (Volume), Medium-Term (Content), Short-Term (Acute and Largely Random)

**What it is** — From Sirenko's study and "other studies of the influence of training loads on functional indicators," the authors identify "three levels of change in an athlete's fitness state during training" (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image):
1. "A long-term level characterised by the steady rise in the athlete's special work-capacity," over "one or more years," based on "long-term adaptation, promoted chiefly by the volume of loading."
2. "A medium-term level characterised by less stable and readily reversible functional changes, the basis for which is compensatory adaptation," over "lengthy training stages of up to 5-6 months," produced with volume by "the characteristics of its contents, in particular, the proportion of intensive means in the total volume of loading."
3. "A short-term level characterised by brief, but not precisely measurable, changes in the functional indicators," the "acute reaction to the training load" within the microcycle, elicited by "the magnitude of the load, the intensity of loading, the individual ability of the athlete to endure the loading and his restorative capabilities." "At this level, the dynamics of the functional indicators are largely random and at times unpredictable. This level is not determined by the adaptation of the first two levels and is important only for organisation of the microcycle and achievement of the immediate effect of the current loading."

Their conclusion: "the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state during the annual cycle are controllable," so training should be built "by first of all taking into account the dynamics of the athlete's special physical preparedness (SPP)" (PDF p. 378). "The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time"; "Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, text layer; page image not opened).

**Why it works** — The authors say the dependence of fitness on load "is determined by definite adaptive processes" and name the basis of each level (long-term adaptation, compensatory adaptation, acute reaction). They do not explain why the short-term level is independent of the other two.

**When to apply** — Deciding which signal to act on: microcycle-level swings guide the week's organisation only; stage-level trends reflect the content and share of intensive means; year-on-year trends reflect volume. Eric's baseline: "Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 64, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: that split maps onto the authors' levels 1-2 versus level 3. Eric's baseline: daily jumps "build the rolling baseline and SWC; Wednesday is the single decision read that changes the week" (line 255, Tension 12 status, resolved 2026-10-02 by Eric). Inference: using a rolling baseline and SWC is one way to separate the "largely random" short-term level from a real trend.

**When NOT to apply** — The time spans (one or more years, up to 5-6 months, microcycle) are given without data. The claim that timing a peak is "not especially complex" is cited to unnamed research ("Research shows"), with no study named. Inference: calling short-term changes "not precisely measurable" reflects the authors' tools; it does not by itself mean modern daily testing carries no signal, though the authors would limit its use to microcycle decisions.

**Example** — The authors' own anchor: Sirenko's (1980) middle-distance runners, where the same running volume with a different distribution of strength means changed the stage-level and competition results ([[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]]; PDF p. 378). Inference: a drop in one Wednesday mRSI read after a heavy Monday is level-3 noise unless it persists across reads; a decline across a six-week stage points to the stage's content.

**Related** — [[claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification]], [[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]], [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--general-prep-stage-duration-must-match-sports-form-cycle]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]]

=================== claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification.md
# Over a Year, Speed-Strength Moves Randomly at Medium Qualification, Follows the Plan in Developing Athletes, and Defies the Plan in the Highly Qualified

**What it is** — The authors say "there is very little research concerning the dynamics of the athlete's state over the annual cycle," and that "Research assessing the athlete's state 3 to 4 times a year is not very informative, since the most interesting changes in state occur between each of these stages." Laboratory studies of untrained subjects over 3-4 months (Pollock 1973) are "of little use in programming the training of highly qualified athletes." "Therefore, Verkhoshansky and his colleagues undertook research ... under the natural conditions of training athletes of various levels of qualification, recording functional indicators twice a month and correlating all changes with calculations of the training loads and volumes" (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366, checked against the page image; the third-person naming marks this framing as Siff's). The findings, for "sports requiring explosive force" (PDF pp. 377-378, checked against the page images):
- **Medium qualification.** "random increases in speed-strength ... together with insignificant changes in speed-strength during the annual cycle," fluctuations that "often do not conform to the periodisation schemes of training or the competition calendar." The stated cause: "complex training (i.e. the concurrent use of loading regimes of different primary emphasis) and the monotonous monthly distribution of the general volume of loading."
- **Non-elite athletes as proficiency grows.** "a trend towards regularity which reflects the type of training periodisation": in a monocycle (e.g. decathlon) special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations"; in a bi-cycle, "two large waves" ending in the winter and summer competitions.
- **Highly qualified athletes.** Dynamics "cannot be regulated in such a manner." "Large fluctuations in speed-strength preparedness can be of different duration and magnitude, can occur at different stages of the annual cycle and often show neither a logical correlation with traditional periodisation of training (for the given sport) nor the competition calendar."

**Why it works** — For the medium-qualification pattern the authors give the cause quoted above (complex training plus a monotonous monthly volume). For the highly qualified pattern they give no cause in this passage; the next paragraph points to unequal loading of different muscle groups as one source ([[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]]).

**When to apply** — Choosing a testing cadence and reading the results. Inference: by this passage, testing 3-4 times a year misses the changes that matter, and twice a month was the authors' working cadence. Eric's baseline: "Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 59, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "There is no common testing cadence across sports; each sport keeps its own schedule" (line 60, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)). Inference: the authors' twice-monthly figure is a floor a sport-by-sport schedule could be checked against. For a medium-level squad with flat, random-looking results, the authors' diagnosis points to concurrent mixed loading with an even monthly volume.

**When NOT to apply** — No sample sizes, sports or data plots are given in this section; the results are said to appear "throughout Chapter 5 and this chapter." For highly qualified athletes the passage describes irregularity without offering a rule to control it, while the same section concludes that annual dynamics "are controllable" (PDF p. 378); Inference: the two are reconciled only if control comes from the content and organisation of loading rather than from periodisation labels, which is the authors' wider argument. The categories "medium qualification," "non-elite" and "highly qualified" are Soviet classification levels and do not map cleanly onto college rosters.

**Example** — The authors' own: under monocyclic periodisation in the decathlon, special-strength preparedness "generally increases without any significant fluctuations throughout the year," while bi-cyclic plans show two waves ending in the winter and summer competitions (PDF p. 377 / printed p. 366).

**Related** — [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high]], [[claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[claim--time-limits-of-single-emphasis-loading-by-motor-quality]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]

=================== case-study--triple-jumper-plantarflexors-depressed-while-thigh-extensors-high.md
# Triple Jumpers: Jumps Plus Barbell Work Depress the Plantarflexors While the Thigh Extensors Read High

**What it is** — Observing annual dynamics, the authors report that "the speed-strength of thigh extension, knee extension and plantarflexion can show different trends of change at certain training stages" (italics in the original), with "the dynamics of the explosive strength of triple jumpers" as the example (Verkhoshansky 1988; PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image). "The concurrent use of jumping and barbell exercises exerts a more intense local influence on the plantarflexors than other muscles of the lower extremity and, consequently, depresses their functional state. However, the loading is not as intense on the thigh extensors, so that their functional indicators reflect a high value. In this case, the athlete notices that movement coordination is difficult although, on the whole, he feels perfectly fit." Their prescription: when means are chosen without regard to "the differences in their primary emphasis on the specific muscle groups," the muscles' state may not match the sport's needs, harming "technical preparation" and "preparedness for competition," so "it is necessary to regulate the emphasis of the loading on the plantarflexors, and periodically decrease the loading on them, especially during the technical and immediate pre-competition training stages" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is unequal local load: the jump-plus-barbell combination hits the plantarflexors harder than the thigh extensors (PDF p. 378). They give no data on the size or timing of the difference and no physiological mechanism beyond that.

**When to apply** — When an athlete reports that coordination feels off while overall fitness feels fine, or when a whole-leg test looks normal but jumping technique is deteriorating. Eric's baseline: daily CMJ mRSI is the department's readiness marker (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a two-leg CMJ is driven heavily by the hip and knee extensors, so by this case a depressed plantarflexor state could hide behind a normal CMJ; a calf-specific test would be the place to look. Eric's baseline: "The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks 'Mid-Thigh Pull' setting" (line 78, Inferred (protocol)). Inference: that existing test could check this case, though the book does not mention isometric testing for it.

**When NOT to apply** — One cited observation in one event, with no numbers shown in the text; treat it as a hypothesis. Inference: whether a CMJ would miss the plantarflexor drop is untested here; the book does not discuss jump tests in this passage.

**Example** — The authors' own: triple jumpers doing concurrent jumping and barbell work, whose plantarflexors were depressed while thigh-extensor indicators read high, and who reported difficult coordination while feeling fit; the fix was to cut plantarflexor loading periodically, above all in technical and pre-competition stages (PDF p. 378).

**Related** — [[claim--annual-speed-strength-dynamics-depend-on-qualification]], [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]] (plantarflexor strength as an outcome), [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]

59	=================== framework--temporal-and-qualitative-forms-of-the-training-effect.md
60	# Training Effect by Time and by Quality: Short-Term and Long-Term Delayed Effects; Transient, Accumulated, Positive and Negative Cumulative Effects
61	
62	**What it is** — The authors start from the common chain "Acute TE > Delayed TE > Cumulative TE" (Zatsiorsky 1964; Volkov 1966; Matveyev 1977), call it "one-sided" because it ignores "the qualitative changes in the TE when they are produced by training loads of different primary emphasis," and add that "the accumulation of training effects is not simply a summation of separate effects, but a synergistic whole (i.e. the sum of the parts is greater than the whole)" (PDF p. 364 / printed p. 353, checked against the page image; the parenthesis is printed that way; Inference: it appears to state the reverse of what is meant). They then separate "partial TE (the result of the effect of loading of one primary emphasis or means)" from "cumulative TE (the result of the generalised effect on the body of loading of different primary emphasis, applied concurrently or sequentially)" (same page), and propose assessing the TE on "two criteria: the temporal (acute and delayed) and the qualitative (partial and cumulative)" (PDF p. 365 / printed p. 354):
63	- **Temporal.** The acute TE is "observed immediately during or directly after a training session." The delayed TE appears either "a relatively short time after the loading, for example, in a number of mixed sessions or over a short period (the short-term TE), or preserved for a longer time after the loading imposed over prolonged training stages (the long-term TE)" (PDF pp. 365-366). The text says the long-term TE "is analysed more thoroughly later (see 6.8)"; the analysis is in 6.10 (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).
64	- **Qualitative forms of the cumulative TE** (Fig 6.26, PDF p. 366 / printed p. 355, checked against the page image): "transient (the body's immediate reaction to a complex of training influences of different emphasis, imposed in one or mixed workouts, as well as the prolonged, parallel use of loading of different emphasis)"; "accumulated (the stratification of traces of the training loads of different emphasis, following in a certain order in prolonged training stages)"; and "positive or negative (if the traces of some loads create or, conversely, do not create favourable conditions for adaptation to other loading)." In the figure, the short-term and long-term effects and both the transient and accumulated effects each carry a positive/negative branch.
65	
66	The cumulative TE depends on "the current state of fitness, the order in which training regimes of different emphasis follow each other, the after-effects of preceding loading, and the duration of given training means (Verkhoshansky, 1970)" (PDF p. 364). The authors defend the scheme: "At first glance, this classification of the TE may appear to be somewhat tedious," but "the programming of training loads should be based primarily on the objective of achieving a definite TE" (PDF p. 366).
67	
68	**Why it works** — The authors' stated basis is "The mechanism of generalised adaptation," described as "the automatic selection of an accommodative strategy which is most appropriate in that situation," involving "selective response to the training influences of different primary emphasis and their stable integration into a well-adapted system" (PDF p. 364). That is a general statement, not a tested mechanism.
69	
70	**When to apply** — Labelling what a block is meant to produce before choosing its content: concurrent loading within a stage gives a transient effect; ordered stages give an accumulated effect; each can be positive or negative. Inference: rotating emphasis every two weeks lands in the transient category by the authors' own later rule ([[heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive]]). Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities ... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the positive/negative branch is the book's vocabulary for that compatibility question.
71	
72	**When NOT to apply** — This is a classification, not a protocol; it gives no test for telling a transient from an accumulated effect in a real athlete. The authors themselves say research on the forms of the TE "is very contradictory" (PDF p. 364). It extends rather than replaces the 4.1.2 taxonomy ([[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]); "partial" here is that entry's "particular." Zatsiorsky's library entry uses a different three-way scheme ([[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/principle--two-factor-fitness-fatigue-theory-and-training-effects-taxonomy]]), and Bompa another ([[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]]); Inference: the terms do not map one to one across the three books.
73	
74	**Example** — The authors' own: in Fig 6.24, barbell exercises then depth jumps gave "a positive cumulative TE," the reverse "a negative cumulative TE," and concurrent use a larger first-stage effect that then fell (PDF pp. 364-365; [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]]).

80	=================== heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation.md
81	# Restoration Means Help When Organised With the Load, but Routine Artificial Restoration Can Blunt Adaptation
82	
83	**What it is** — The authors give GPP means a restorative role, important "in those sports in which there are few supplementary training means and training is inherently monotonous ... (gymnastics, weightlifting and cyclic sports)" (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357, checked against the page image). Two reported gains: with "the sole and systematic use of swimming restoration procedures during the execution of voluminous loading," absolute strength rose 24.2% and strength-endurance 18.9%, against 7.7% and 4.9% in swimmers without them, while training volume rose "by an average of 15%" (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980); and in highly qualified middle-distance runners before competition, "low frequency vibromassage and psycho-regulatory training" raised training-distance speed by 2-4% and volume at competition speed by 12-20% (Potapchenko 1979). They conclude that "the organised combination of training loads and restorative procedures is an important prerequisite for intensifying and increasing the effectiveness of training" (same page).
84	
85	Then the limit: "restoration after work is a natural process which occurs in a definite sequence over a certain period" (Yakovlev 1971). "Artificially accelerating the restoration process as a routine can disturb the natural course of the body's long-term adaptation to intense muscular activity and therefore can be justified only in clear cases of over-exertion (Siff & Yessis, 1992)." "Frequent and regular application of non-specific means of restoration may hinder the adaptation process, especially when large training loads are used," and "premature intervention during the course of restoration can hinder the body's supercompensatory ability to enhance this process by natural means (Yevgenyev et al, 1975)." The loading-restoration process "should be strictly regulated on the basis of scientific assessment of the athlete's fitness state" (PDF p. 368).
86	
87	**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "Increasing the volume and intensity of the loading disturbs homeostasis as a basic condition for promoting adaptation to loading and enhancement of the restoration processes" (PDF p. 368). Removing that disturbance too early removes part of the signal. No study is described in enough detail to test the warning.
88	
89	**When to apply** — Deciding when to use restoration modalities: plan them as part of the load when the aim is to raise training volume, and avoid them as a daily routine after every hard session, keeping them for "clear cases of over-exertion." Eric's baseline: "Recovery capacity must be 'earned' by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the authors' last sentence asks for restoration to be regulated on an assessment of fitness state, which the baseline says is not done; the mRSI read (line 74) is the nearest existing measure.
90	
91	**When NOT to apply** — The positive data and the warning sit side by side without a rule for telling "organised combination" from "routine" use. The reported gains carry no sample sizes or statistics, and the Kuchnyev result confounds restoration with a 15% rise in volume. Inference: the warning names "non-specific means" and "artificially accelerating" restoration; it does not address sleep or nutrition.
92	**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers using systematic restoration procedures during high-volume loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them, while also handling about 15% more volume (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980; PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357).
93	
94	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules]] (restorative procedures in the microcycle), [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]]

98	=================== claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks.md
99	# Endurance Athletes Need Specialised Strength and Jump Work: The Authors' 800 m Benchmarks
100	
101	**What it is** — The authors argue that "the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work invariably is underestimated" and that "specialisation of the muscles, as the direct executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning." Long-duration work alone can leave "a definite imbalance" between cardiorespiratory function and "the working potential of the muscles," and then "the anticipated sporting proficiency will not result" (PDF pp. 367-368 / printed pp. 356-357, checked against the page images). Their illustration: "This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" (PDF p. 368). The remedy: "specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance training," raising local muscular endurance including "'anaerobic' energy production," so that "it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982)" (same page). Such work should "firstly increase strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing repeated motor actions"; "The main thing is to overcome the archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone" (same page). Earlier, in italics: "It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is not the fundamental and sole task of strength training" (PDF p. 367).
102	
103	**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: strength and jump work loads the muscles harder than distance running, "thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves," enhancing "the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes" (PDF p. 368).
104	
105	**When to apply** — Endurance or mixed-demand athletes whose conditioning is mostly long-duration running: add specialised strength and jump work aimed at repeated efforts, and expect to need less glycolytic volume. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery ... not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors make the converse point for endurance athletes, that strength and power support the endurance event; together they argue against treating strength and conditioning as separate silos, as does the baseline's "Everything we do is some form of conditioning" (line 122, Explicit).
106	
107	**When NOT to apply** — The 800 m benchmarks are introduced as "Elementary logic decrees"; they are asserted, not measured, and no study links the jump distances to 800 m performance. The cited studies are named without data. Inference: the benchmarks are for elite men's 800 m (1:45.0) and say nothing about lower standards or women's events.
108	
109	**Example** — The authors' own: an 800 m runner aiming at 1:45.0 should, by their reasoning, be able to run 100 m in 10.6-10.7 s and cover at least 9 m in three consecutive standing long jumps or 33-34 m in ten, which "middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" to do (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357).
110	
111	**Related** — [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]], [[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (Fig 6.30, ten-jump gains in middle-distance runners after a strength block)

=================== case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners.md
# Sirenko (1980): Same Running, Two Concentrated Strength Peaks Instead of One, Better 800 m and 1500 m Gains

**What it is** — To show that a runner's aerobic and anaerobic state "depends on the contents and organisation of the training loads," the authors report Sirenko (1980): two groups of middle-distance runners over an annual cycle, each with "the same volume and distribution of running means," but "Group 1 used a traditional single-peak distribution of strength-means, whereas Group 2 used a double-peaked distribution of means with the emphasis concentrated in December and March-April" (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, checked against the page image). "Group 2 proved superior in all tests of functional ability, including aerobic efficiency, 'anaerobic threshold' (onset of blood lactate accumulation) and the results of control runs of 400m and 1200m, as well as in their sporting performances. During the summer competition stage Group 2 improved the 800m time by an average of 4.8 seconds and the 1500m run by 6.3 seconds, whereas in Group 1, the improvements were 3.4 and 4.6 seconds, respectively" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors present the study as evidence that content and organisation, not running volume alone, set the fitness state; they give no mechanism for why two concentrated strength peaks beat one. Inference: it fits their account of concentrated loading and the delayed rise that follows it ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]), and the LDTE of concentrated strength loading in middle-distance runners that they report from Zhdanovich (1980) on PDF p. 374.

**When to apply** — Planning strength work for endurance athletes with two competition seasons: concentrate the strength means before each, rather than spreading them in one long wave. Inference: the design held running constant, so it isolates the strength distribution, which makes it a cleaner case than most in the chapter.

**When NOT to apply** — The book gives no group sizes, athlete level, statistics or description of the strength means themselves. "Single-peak" and "double-peaked" describe the shape of the strength-means curve over the year; the timing of the single peak is not given. Inference: the result is in middle-distance runners with winter and summer seasons; it does not directly address a sport with one long competitive season such as college football.

**Example** — The authors' own: Group 2 (strength means concentrated in December and March-April) improved 800 m by an average of 4.8 s and 1500 m by 6.3 s in the summer competition stage, against 3.4 s and 4.6 s for Group 1 (PDF p. 378).

**Related** — [[claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--three-levels-of-change-in-fitness-state]], [[claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks]], [[claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains]] (also cites Sirenko), [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]]
