=================== case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers.md
# High Jumpers (Fig 6.24): Barbell Then Depth Jumps Beat the Reverse; Concurrent Use Wins the First Stage, Then Fades

**What it is** — To separate partial from cumulative training effects, the authors describe an experiment in which "group 1 began by using barbell exercises, followed by depth-jumps ... Group 2 used the reverse sequence of means. Each group of means were used for three months each. Group 3 used the barbell exercises and the depth-jumps concurrently throughout both 3-month stages. The overall volume of the loading was equivalent in all groups" (PDF p. 364 / printed p. 353, checked against the page image). The caption names the athletes as "high jumpers of medium qualification" (PDF p. 365 / printed p. 354). The three conclusions (PDF pp. 364-365, checked against the page images):
1. "The partial TE of the depth-jumping is greater than that of the barbell exercises."
2. "The sequence of using barbell exercises followed by depth-jumps (group 1) produced a higher level of speed-strength preparedness (a positive cumulative TE), than the reverse sequence (group 2). In group 2 the TE was essentially lower at the end of the second stage than after the first (a negative cumulative TE)."
3. "The concurrent use of the above means in the first stage (group 3) yielded a larger cumulative effect than in groups 1 and 2. However, the TE noticeably decreased for group 3 during the second stage because the lengthy use of a single means decreases the training potential of the loading."

**Figure 6.24 values** (read by eye from a 300 dpi crop of PDF p. 365; white bar after the first 3 months, shaded bar after the next 3): absolute strength GP1 about 36 then 54, GP2 about 50 then 45, GP3 about 63 then 53; explosive strength GP1 about 54 then 102, GP2 about 88 then 78, GP3 about 123 then 96; vertical jump GP1 about 14 then 25, GP2 about 15-16 then 14, GP3 about 33 then 23. At the end, group 1 is about level with or slightly above group 3 on all three measures. **Unclear units:** the caption says "All values in % increase over initial values" and describes graph 1 as plantarflexor absolute strength, graph 2 as "maximal explosive effort in a vertical jump" and graph 3 as "the increase in height after a depth jump," but the panels are titled Absolute Strength (kgf), Explosive Strength (kgf) and Vertical Jump (cm). The numbers above are axis readings; which unit is correct is not stated.

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for group 3's fall is the one quoted: "lengthy use of a single means decreases the training potential of the loading." For the order effect, the companion passage on PDF p. 372 gives their mechanism: extensive resistance work first produces "a rise in the general energy potential of the neuromuscular system," creating "favourable conditions" for the explosive work ([[heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive]]). Inference: group 3 used the two means "concurrently," so "a single means" in conclusion 3 most likely refers to the same complex used for six months; the book does not say.

**When to apply** — Ordering an off-season for jumpers or other speed-strength athletes: heavy resistance stage first, depth-jump stage second; if both are used together, change the complex after one stage rather than running it unchanged for two. Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — No sample sizes, statistics or variance are given, and the unit mismatch above means the size of each change is uncertain. The design matches the Chapter 5 novice experiment 3 almost exactly (weights then depth jumps, the reverse, and both in both stages), but Chapter 5 labels those subjects novices (PDF p. 299 / printed p. 288; [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]]) while this figure says high jumpers of medium qualification. Inference: they may be the same study described twice or two studies; the book does not say, and the researcher names partly overlap (Khodykin and Chernousov are cited on PDF p. 364 and named in the Chapter 5 list). The two accounts agree on direction. Inference: group 3's first-stage advantage reads against the authors' advice elsewhere to concentrate rather than mix for highly qualified athletes, but these subjects were of medium qualification, for whom the authors say concurrent and distributed approaches both work (PDF p. 371).

**Example** — The authors' own: after the second 3-month stage, the barbell-first group reached about 102 on explosive strength against about 78 for the depth-jump-first group, whose value had fallen from about 88 after stage 1 (Fig 6.24, PDF p. 365; axis readings, units unclear).

**Related** — [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]], [[heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive]], [[framework--temporal-and-qualitative-forms-of-the-training-effect]], [[case-study--nedobyvailov-light-heavy-and-combined-loads-in-jumpers]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]], [[case-study--deniskin-depth-jumps-after-resistance-and-rest-as-a-training-means]], [[framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]

# Nedobyvailov (Fig 6.25): 30-50% 1RM Gave the Most Speed, 70-90% the Most Strength, Combined 30-90% the Most Power

**What it is** — "over a 7-week period, group 1 used weights exercises with 30-50% of 1RM; group 2 used 70-90% of 1RM and group 3 used weights of 30-90% of 1RM concurrently (i.e. using the 30-50% and 70-90% regimes together). The general loading in all groups was equivalent in terms of the metabolic cost of the work" (PDF p. 365 / printed p. 354, checked against the page image). The caption: "The training effect (in % increase) of different loading schemes on highly qualified jumpers for the extensor muscles of both legs (Nedobyvailov)." The authors point to "how the cumulative phenomenon appears as a result of combination work with weights of 30-90% of 1RM regarding the power achieved in group 3, and how much higher it is relative to the partial TE obtained with means of single emphasis," and add that "the greatest increase in speed was produced by training with loads of 30-50% of 1RM (Group 1, graph 2)" (same page).

**Figure 6.25 values** (read by eye from a 300 dpi crop of PDF p. 365, % increase): absolute strength GP1 about 7, GP2 about 18-19, GP3 about 17; speed GP1 about 18-19, GP2 about 11-12, GP3 about 14; power GP1 about 6-7, GP2 about 15, GP3 about 21.

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism; they present the result as an example of a cumulative effect being more than either partial effect. Inference: in these bars the combined group sits near the heavy group on strength and between the two on speed, so its power lead fits a product of both; that reading is not in the book.

**When to apply** — When power is the target, the authors' data favour mixing light (30-50%) and heavy (70-90%) loads over either alone; when pure speed is the target, light loads did best. Eric's baseline: "The dynamic strength index (DSI ...) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21); the baseline tags it contested, "one controlled trial (Pleša 2024, basketball, split at 0.90) supported only the strength arm; no football data"). Inference: this experiment is another case where mixing the heavy and light ends beat either single emphasis on power, which argues for a mixed default when the DSI read is ambiguous.

**When NOT to apply** — Seven weeks, "highly qualified jumpers," leg extensors only; no sample size, statistics, exercises or test methods are given, and "speed" and "power" are not defined. Volume was equated by "metabolic cost," which the authors do not explain. Inference: group 3's absolute-strength gain (about 17%) was close to the heavy-only group's (about 18-19%), so in this figure mixing did not cost strength; that may not hold with less training time.

**Example** — The authors' own: power rose about 21% in the 30-90% group against about 15% (70-90%) and about 6-7% (30-50%), while speed rose most, about 18-19%, with 30-50% loads (Fig 6.25, PDF p. 365).

**Related** — [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]], [[framework--temporal-and-qualitative-forms-of-the-training-effect]], [[heuristic--within-session-order-of-explosive-means-matters-less-than-volume-and-contrast]] (lists barbell work at 30% and 90% as a positive pairing), [[heuristic--speed-strength-loading-light-loads-maximal-acceleration-and-5-to-1-mix]], [[claim--power-output-peaks-then-declines-with-load-jump-vs-leg-press]], [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]

# Training Effect by Time and by Quality: Short-Term and Long-Term Delayed Effects; Transient, Accumulated, Positive and Negative Cumulative Effects

**What it is** — The authors start from the common chain "Acute TE > Delayed TE > Cumulative TE" (Zatsiorsky 1964; Volkov 1966; Matveyev 1977), call it "one-sided" because it ignores "the qualitative changes in the TE when they are produced by training loads of different primary emphasis," and add that "the accumulation of training effects is not simply a summation of separate effects, but a synergistic whole (i.e. the sum of the parts is greater than the whole)" (PDF p. 364 / printed p. 353, checked against the page image; the parenthesis is printed that way; Inference: it appears to state the reverse of what is meant). They then separate "partial TE (the result of the effect of loading of one primary emphasis or means)" from "cumulative TE (the result of the generalised effect on the body of loading of different primary emphasis, applied concurrently or sequentially)" (same page), and propose assessing the TE on "two criteria: the temporal (acute and delayed) and the qualitative (partial and cumulative)" (PDF p. 365 / printed p. 354):
- **Temporal.** The acute TE is "observed immediately during or directly after a training session." The delayed TE appears either "a relatively short time after the loading, for example, in a number of mixed sessions or over a short period (the short-term TE), or preserved for a longer time after the loading imposed over prolonged training stages (the long-term TE)" (PDF pp. 365-366). The text says the long-term TE "is analysed more thoroughly later (see 6.8)"; the analysis is in 6.10 (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).
- **Qualitative forms of the cumulative TE** (Fig 6.26, PDF p. 366 / printed p. 355, checked against the page image): "transient (the body's immediate reaction to a complex of training influences of different emphasis, imposed in one or mixed workouts, as well as the prolonged, parallel use of loading of different emphasis)"; "accumulated (the stratification of traces of the training loads of different emphasis, following in a certain order in prolonged training stages)"; and "positive or negative (if the traces of some loads create or, conversely, do not create favourable conditions for adaptation to other loading)." In the figure, the short-term and long-term effects and both the transient and accumulated effects each carry a positive/negative branch.

The cumulative TE depends on "the current state of fitness, the order in which training regimes of different emphasis follow each other, the after-effects of preceding loading, and the duration of given training means (Verkhoshansky, 1970)" (PDF p. 364). The authors defend the scheme: "At first glance, this classification of the TE may appear to be somewhat tedious," but "the programming of training loads should be based primarily on the objective of achieving a definite TE" (PDF p. 366).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated basis is "The mechanism of generalised adaptation," described as "the automatic selection of an accommodative strategy which is most appropriate in that situation," involving "selective response to the training influences of different primary emphasis and their stable integration into a well-adapted system" (PDF p. 364). That is a general statement, not a tested mechanism.

**When to apply** — Labelling what a block is meant to produce before choosing its content: concurrent loading within a stage gives a transient effect; ordered stages give an accumulated effect; each can be positive or negative. Inference: rotating emphasis every two weeks lands in the transient category by the authors' own later rule ([[heuristic--sequential-accumulation-needs-4-6-week-stages-extensive-before-explosive]]). Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities ... are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the positive/negative branch is the book's vocabulary for that compatibility question.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a classification, not a protocol; it gives no test for telling a transient from an accumulated effect in a real athlete. The authors themselves say research on the forms of the TE "is very contradictory" (PDF p. 364). It extends rather than replaces the 4.1.2 taxonomy ([[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]); "partial" here is that entry's "particular." Zatsiorsky's library entry uses a different three-way scheme ([[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/principle--two-factor-fitness-fatigue-theory-and-training-effects-taxonomy]]), and Bompa another ([[periodization--bompa/framework--three-training-effects]]); Inference: the terms do not map one to one across the three books.

**Example** — The authors' own: in Fig 6.24, barbell exercises then depth jumps gave "a positive cumulative TE," the reverse "a negative cumulative TE," and concurrent use a larger first-stage effect that then fell (PDF pp. 364-365; [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]]).

=================== heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation.md
# Restoration Means Help When Organised With the Load, but Routine Artificial Restoration Can Blunt Adaptation

**What it is** — The authors give GPP means a restorative role, important "in those sports in which there are few supplementary training means and training is inherently monotonous ... (gymnastics, weightlifting and cyclic sports)" (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357, checked against the page image). Two reported gains: with "the sole and systematic use of swimming restoration procedures during the execution of voluminous loading," absolute strength rose 24.2% and strength-endurance 18.9%, against 7.7% and 4.9% in swimmers without them, while training volume rose "by an average of 15%" (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980); and in highly qualified middle-distance runners before competition, "low frequency vibromassage and psycho-regulatory training" raised training-distance speed by 2-4% and volume at competition speed by 12-20% (Potapchenko 1979). They conclude that "the organised combination of training loads and restorative procedures is an important prerequisite for intensifying and increasing the effectiveness of training" (same page).

Then the limit: "restoration after work is a natural process which occurs in a definite sequence over a certain period" (Yakovlev 1971). "Artificially accelerating the restoration process as a routine can disturb the natural course of the body's long-term adaptation to intense muscular activity and therefore can be justified only in clear cases of over-exertion (Siff & Yessis, 1992)." "Frequent and regular application of non-specific means of restoration may hinder the adaptation process, especially when large training loads are used," and "premature intervention during the course of restoration can hinder the body's supercompensatory ability to enhance this process by natural means (Yevgenyev et al, 1975)." The loading-restoration process "should be strictly regulated on the basis of scientific assessment of the athlete's fitness state" (PDF p. 368).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "Increasing the volume and intensity of the loading disturbs homeostasis as a basic condition for promoting adaptation to loading and enhancement of the restoration processes" (PDF p. 368). Removing that disturbance too early removes part of the signal. No study is described in enough detail to test the warning.

**When to apply** — Deciding when to use restoration modalities: plan them as part of the load when the aim is to raise training volume, and avoid them as a daily routine after every hard session, keeping them for "clear cases of over-exertion." Eric's baseline: "Recovery capacity must be 'earned' by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 151, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: the authors' last sentence asks for restoration to be regulated on an assessment of fitness state, which the baseline says is not done; the mRSI read (line 74) is the nearest existing measure.

**When NOT to apply** — The positive data and the warning sit side by side without a rule for telling "organised combination" from "routine" use. The reported gains carry no sample sizes or statistics, and the Kuchnyev result confounds restoration with a 15% rise in volume. Inference: the warning names "non-specific means" and "artificially accelerating" restoration; it does not address sleep or nutrition.
**Example** — The authors' own: swimmers using systematic restoration procedures during high-volume loading gained 24.2% in absolute strength and 18.9% in strength-endurance, against 7.7% and 4.9% without them, while also handling about 15% more volume (Kuchnyev 1977; Platonov 1980; PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357).

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--microcycle-construction-key-workout-rules]] (restorative procedures in the microcycle), [[framework--supplementary-readiness-markers-hr-bp-ceff-palpation]]

=================== claim--middle-distance-runners-need-strength-and-jump-training-benchmarks.md
# Endurance Athletes Need Specialised Strength and Jump Work: The Authors' 800 m Benchmarks

**What it is** — The authors argue that "the importance of muscular adaptation to intense and prolonged work invariably is underestimated" and that "specialisation of the muscles, as the direct executor of the work, is of greater significance than development of the cardiovascular-respiratory component of endurance. A more intense stimulus is necessary for promoting adaptation of the muscles to endurance work than for producing cardiovascular and respiratory conditioning." Long-duration work alone can leave "a definite imbalance" between cardiorespiratory function and "the working potential of the muscles," and then "the anticipated sporting proficiency will not result" (PDF pp. 367-368 / printed pp. 356-357, checked against the page images). Their illustration: "This situation is very typical of the preparation of middle-distance runners. Elementary logic decrees that in order to run 800m in 1:45:0, it is necessary to be able to achieve a time of 10.6-10.7 seconds in the 100m. One needs to possess great strength potential to do this, e.g. the ability to execute three consecutive standing long jumps covering a total distance of at least 9m, or ten consecutive standing long jumps totalling 33-34m, for which middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" (PDF p. 368). The remedy: "specialised strength and jump training which exerts a stronger influence on the muscles than distance training," raising local muscular endurance including "'anaerobic' energy production," so that "it is possible to reduce the volume of exhausting endurance work in the 'anaerobic' glycolytic zone (Zhdanovich, 1980; Verkhoshansky & Sirenko, 1982)" (same page). Such work should "firstly increase strength up to a definite optimum, and secondly, exploit the specific energy processes crucial for producing repeated motor actions"; "The main thing is to overcome the archaic viewpoint which regards strength training as a means of increasing absolute strength alone" (same page). Earlier, in italics: "It is undoubtedly important to increase strength, but this is not the fundamental and sole task of strength training" (PDF p. 367).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: strength and jump work loads the muscles harder than distance running, "thereby intensifying their adaptation to endurance work and activating the relevant functional reserves," enhancing "the power and the capacity of the metabolic processes" (PDF p. 368).

**When to apply** — Endurance or mixed-demand athletes whose conditioning is mostly long-duration running: add specialised strength and jump work aimed at repeated efforts, and expect to need less glycolytic volume. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery ... not distance capacity" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors make the converse point for endurance athletes, that strength and power support the endurance event; together they argue against treating strength and conditioning as separate silos, as does the baseline's "Everything we do is some form of conditioning" (line 122, Explicit).

**When NOT to apply** — The 800 m benchmarks are introduced as "Elementary logic decrees"; they are asserted, not measured, and no study links the jump distances to 800 m performance. The cited studies are named without data. Inference: the benchmarks are for elite men's 800 m (1:45.0) and say nothing about lower standards or women's events.

**Example** — The authors' own: an 800 m runner aiming at 1:45.0 should, by their reasoning, be able to run 100 m in 10.6-10.7 s and cover at least 9 m in three consecutive standing long jumps or 33-34 m in ten, which "middle-distance runners usually do not have the strength" to do (PDF p. 368 / printed p. 357).

**Related** — [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[claim--strength-training-raises-haemoglobin-myoglobin-and-aids-distance-sport]], [[case-study--sirenko-double-peak-strength-means-for-middle-distance-runners]], [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (Fig 6.30, ten-jump gains in middle-distance runners after a strength block)

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

content.content:
== 59: - Weekly tracking is preferred over infrequent (e.g., once-a-phase) testing, specifically to catch plateaus or declines early enough to adjust programming. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7] (See the cadence bullet below: there is no department-wide cadence.)
== 60: - There is no common testing cadence across sports; each sport keeps its own schedule. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q9): "We currently don't have a consistent cadence across all sports. Individual sports have their own unique schedules." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q9)**
== 64: - Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
== 74: - Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
== 75: - The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds, not a single cut-off or position-group thresholds. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2): "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized." Individualized against: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)** Inference: "should be" may describe the intended rule rather than a fully running one; no numeric threshold was given. See Tension 12 (daily testing v
== 76: - The dynamic strength index (DSI: CMJ against isometric mid-thigh pull peak force) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q21): "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** This is not the SJ-CMJ gap the question asked about. Evidence check done 2026-09-29 (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`): cite it as Eric's practice, tagged [contested; the ratio track
== 78: - The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
== 101: - The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + shared course material) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
== 104: - Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
== 105: - Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21] Not claimed in the interview. The in-season dose itself is unknown: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps."
== 106: - Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use") [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
== 114: - All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
== 116: - For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the interview, **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**
== 117: - Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
== 122: - "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
== 123: - For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
== 124: - Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
== 142: - Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
== 151: - Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
== 153: - Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**
== 180: - The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
== 182: - Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
== 185: - In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
== 186: - The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**
== 255:     **Status: RESOLVED 2026-10-02 (Eric).** Daily jumps are collected to build the rolling baseline and SWC; Wednesday is the single decision read that changes the week.

== 64: - Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
== 74: - Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
== 75: - The mRSI decision read happens on Wednesdays, against individualized thresholds, not a single cut-off or position-group thresholds. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2): "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized." Individualized against: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a): "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)** Inference: "should be" may describe the intended rule rather than a fully running one; no numeric threshold was given. See Tension 12 (daily testing v
== 76: - The dynamic strength index (DSI: CMJ against isometric mid-thigh pull peak force) chooses between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q21): "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** This is not the SJ-CMJ gap the question asked about. Evidence check done 2026-09-29 (`docs/synthesis/_work/dsi-evidence-check.md`): cite it as Eric's practice, tagged [contested; the ratio track
== 78: - The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps. **Inferred (protocol)** [protocol-iso-seated-calf-raise.md; revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md]
== 101: - The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + shared course material) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
== 104: - Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.13; week1-lecture.md p.31]
== 105: - Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work. In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule. **Inferred (transcript + shared slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.20-21; hhpr-5355-class-8-2026.md p.21] Not claimed in the interview. The in-season dose itself is unknown: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q18): "I don't have the specific sets and reps."
== 106: - Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression, specifically to avoid staleness while still building tolerance for higher loads. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed but first-person: "For me personally, this is a more preferential model to use") [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26]
== 114: - All three energy systems (alactic ~10-12s highest power, glycolytic/anaerobic-lactic ~60-90s medium capacity, aerobic hours-long lowest power/highest capacity) are always active simultaneously; programming targets the adaptation, not the drill label. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.19; class-4-2026.md p.15]
== 116: - For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the interview, **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**
== 117: - Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
== 122: - "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
== 123: - For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
== 124: - Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
== 142: - Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
== 151: - Recovery capacity must be "earned" by training hard enough first; recovery technology (Theragun, Normatec, cryo) is treated as useful but not a substitute for managing training stress and dose correctly. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.9]
== 153: - Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**
== 180: - The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume), before a transition into competition. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.19-21; week1-lecture.md pp.43-48]
== 182: - Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block — "you can't ride two horses with one saddle." Compatible qualities are trained together; the rest are trained at a retention dose. **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.28-29; week1-lecture.md p.70]
== 185: - In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)** He did not say whether the postseason gets a distinct taper.
== 186: - The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)**

=== heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block.md

**What it is** — The authors reject reading block loading as strength only: "*Although there is a primary emphasis on a specific motor quality at different stages of training, this does not mean that technique work is totally omitted during the stage of concentrated strength loading*" (italics in the original; PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371). Their rules (PDF pp. 382-383 / printed pp. 371-372, both checked against the page images):
1. **Daily technique, with freshness for the hard parts.** "One must work on improving technique daily, especially in speed-strength and complex-technical types of sports, with 'freshness' of the body being an important prerequisite for development of technique (Dyachkov, 1966; Ozolin, 1970; Ratov, 1979). Separate tasks of technical training which do not require maximum intensity of effort can be performed with the body in a lowered functional state, but the execution of other tasks under such conditions is unacceptable."
2. **Two stages of technical work in the preparatory period.** "During the first stage, one perfects those *components of technique* which need improvement and during the second, the emphasis is on executing *the sport exercise as a whole* with high intensity of effort" (italics in the original; PDF p. 383). High-intensity whole-skill work "should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period" (PDF p. 382).
3. **During the block: motor learning at low intensity.** One should "primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the concentrated loading... this task is carried out at low intensity," by "special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions" (PDF p. 383).
4. **After the block: perfecting at high intensity.** "During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his increasing speed-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort" (PDF p. 383).
=== framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation.md

**What it is** — "Two forms of compensatory adaptation, associated with enhancing the CAR by systematic training, which differ in volume and organisation of the training loads, have been identified and studied in explosive sports" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image):
- **(A) Distributed loading:** "a gradual increase in the functional indicators," with "a moderate volume of continuous loading." "periodic brief disturbances of the body's homeostasis occur and the current expenditure of energy resources is compensated during training." It "follows traditional concepts for developing trainability and is typical for athletes of medium classification."
- **(B) Concentrated loading:** "a large, concentrated volume of special physical preparation means, concentrated in the first half of the training phase. These large volumes provoke a profound and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which is reflected by decrease of the functional indicators. Then, after the volume of loading is decreased, their increase accelerates and exceeds the level achieved with the first form of adaptation. This way of organising loading in the preparatory mesocycles was devised for highly qualified athletes and has been shown by research to be effective for all types of sport (Verkhoshansky, 1977)."

Fig 6.23, "Two forms of compensatory adaptation during the large preparation phase (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 361 / printed p. 350, checked against the page image and high-resolution crops of both panels), plots % change (100 = start) over 18 weeks, with dashed lines at weeks 6 and 12. Values read by eye, all "about":
=== claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes.md

**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).

Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
=== framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound.md

**What it is** — In 6.12.3 (PDF pp. 385-387 / printed pp. 374-376, all checked against the page images) the authors compare two forms of mesocycle organisation (Fig 6.33, PDF p. 386).

**A terminology warning first.** "In this chapter, *the term 'mesocycle' is reserved for what in Russian is called 'the large stage' or large mesocycle*, which extends over several months to produce a specific adaptive effect... The large mesocycle, in fact, may comprise a few conventional mesocycles and also be referred to as a phase" (italics in the original; PDF p. 385). Its duration "can vary (usually 3-5 months), since its calculation depends on the competition calendar and especially on the dates of the most important competitions" (PDF p. 387).

**Common practice, as the authors report it.** "The literature reveals that three and four week stages are the most frequently used, where the last one week serves as a restoration week. There are combinations of two weeks with heavy loading and two weeks with moderate loading, or an alternation of weeks with high and moderate loading... all of them, depending on circumstances, can produce good results. It is very difficult to establish which of these is the most effective, since the criteria are extremely diverse" (PDF p. 385). Research has concentrated on the annual cycle and the microcycle, plus the "pre-competition training stage lasting 4-6 weeks" (PDF p. 385).
=== heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work.md

**What it is** — Under the heading "More Advanced Use of Concentrated Loading" (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image) the authors modify the separated-block models of 6.14: "in speed-strength sports, the magnitude of the delayed training effect (LDTE) may be enhanced further if the concentrated loading is followed by specialised work of moderate volume, which includes higher power or more explosive muscle contraction regimes, such as jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts." The loads overlap: "There is an overlapping of the different training volumes, which peak smoothly in each case to ensure optimal increase in the LDTE" (PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387). In the bi-cyclic version, "stages A and C refer to concentrated periods of high volume, low intensity work and stages B and D to moderate volumes of specialised, higher intensity speed-strength work. This scheme has been recommended to ensure continuous increase in special strength over a long period (Verkhoshansky, 1978)" (PDF p. 398).

The figures, read from the page images (no numeric axes):
- **Fig 6.43** (PDF p. 398, monocyclic large mesocycle): a tall wave A in the preparatory phase, a smaller wave B starting as A falls and peaking at about the start of the competition phase. The speed-strength curve sags while A is high, then rises through B and keeps rising into the competition phase.
- **Fig 6.44** (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, bi-cyclic): tall A, small B, tall C, small D in sequence. Speed-strength dips during A, rises during B, flattens or dips slightly during C, and rises again after it to its highest level at the right.

=== /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading.md
 Research has shown that unidirectional training over periods as long as 4-12 weeks can be very effective, especially if the intensity is gradually increased for each form of loading in the given cycle.
 Inference: a 4-12 week unidirectional block runs past those windows for the qualities it does not train, so the baseline's retention dose would still be needed alongside it; the authors do not address retention of other qualities here.
=== /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next.md
" The timing: "The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without adequate restoration.
**When to apply** — After any 4-8 week block that concentrates on one quality, plan a lower-load period before the next concentrated block.
 Inference: judge the block's result after the 1-3 week latency, not on the last day of loading.
 Inference: the 1-3 week latency is a reason to leave slack between blocks in that roadmap, so a delayed gain is not cut short by the next block.
**When NOT to apply** — The 1-3 week figure is "most commonly," with no study named.
 It is a latency to the onset of gains.
 Chapter 6 gives a different number for a different quantity: the long-term delayed training effect "was observed to last from 4-12 weeks during the long-term stages of strength preparation," its duration "approximately equal to the duration of the strength training stage," and its appearance "individualised" (PDF p.
 49), and the Bompa entry [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]] repeats this as a 4-12 week delay.
=== /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--delayed-strength-training-effect-lag-before-gains-appear.md
=== /Users/kristinarash/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/strength-and-conditioning/periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching.md
 49); *Supertraining* itself gives a 1-3 week latency before gains appear and 4-12 weeks as how long the delayed effect lasts (see [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]]).
 The delayed-rebound timing (4–12 wk per Bompa & Haff; *Supertraining* gives 1–3 wk to onset) must be planned backward from competition, or the peak lands in the wrong week.

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 6c (6.8.3-6.11), 19 entries

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-10-03, Mac.
Scope: `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch6c.txt` (19 files) in `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, PDF idx 363-379 (printed 352-368), plus PDF 288, 299, 300, 301, 305, 308 and 536.

**What I opened as images** (200 dpi renders in `staging/_renders/r6c_p*.png`, 300 dpi crops for figures): PDF 288, 300 (lower half), 301, 308, 363, 364, 365 (with a 300 dpi crop of Fig 6.25), 366, 367, 368, 369, 370, 371, 372, 373, 374, 375 (with a 300 dpi crop of Fig 6.30), 376, 377, 378, 379, 536. PDF 299 and 305 were checked from the text layer only. Every value below that is read off a graph was measured against the gridlines.

**Also checked:**
- Every "Eric's baseline:" quote against `docs/method-baseline.md` (lines 59, 60, 64, 74, 75, 76, 78, 101, 104, 105, 106, 114, 116, 117, 122, 123, 124, 142, 151, 153, 180, 182, 185, 186, 255). All quotes, line numbers and tags match.
- Every `[[wikilink]]` in the 19 files resolves today in the staging library or the vault, including the links into 6a and 6b.
- Em dashes appear only in the section headers.
- No entry contains review history.

**Fig 6.28** (PDF 369) is a schematic with no numeric axes. No in-scope entry cites it, so there are no values to check.

## Entry table

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum | FIX | (1) **Fig 6.30 block timing is misread.** The entry says the shaded block runs "from about month 1.3 to about month 4.3". On the 300 dpi crop (PDF 375 / p.364), the block runs from about month 1.6 to about month 4.5: left edge 57 px past the month-1 tick at about 98 px per month, right edge about half a month past month 4. The curve values are right: vertical jump about 7 then about 4.5 at month 8; stride about 11; ten jumps about 9-9.5. (2) **"4-12 weeks" has three referents, not two.** The entry's "They are different quantities" sentence names only PDF 374 (5-12 week loading stages) and PDF 375 (LDTE lasts 4-12 weeks). PDF 305 / p.294 also uses "4-12 weeks", for how long unidirectional training "can be very effective". The Addendum, PDF 536 / p.525, attaches 4-12 weeks to *stage length*: "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks". That reading matches the PDF 374 stage figure better than the PDF 375 reading. The source does not agree with itself on what 4-12 weeks measures. | (1) Replace with "during a shaded block from about month 1.6 to about month 4.5". (2) Append to the When NOT sentence: "The book uses 4-12 weeks for three things: how long unidirectional training stays effective (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), how long the LDTE lasts (PDF p. 375), and, in Verkhoshansky's Addendum, the length of the concentrated stages themselves (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525). Keep the locator with the number." Everything else checked: 5-12 weeks and the 4 citations at PDF 374 / p.363; Fig 6.29 shading 0 to about 2.47 months, dips to about 84, 92 and 95%, recross 100 at about month 2.05, month-4 values about 124, 118.5 and 111%; F1, F2 and F3 in Fig 6.31 at PDF 375; maintenance vs LDTE at PDF 377 / p.366 (italic). New angle versus 5c, 4.1.1 and Bompa is confirmed: the dose-response optimum and the maintenance distinction. The 1-3 week latency (PDF 305) and the 4-12 week duration are not restated differently. |
| heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window | FIX | (1) **Wrong voice for the Addendum.** The entry writes "The Addendum restates..." and "**Example** — The authors' own, from the Addendum". The Addendum section is "9.1 Laws of Sports Mastery: Principles of Training, Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis" (PDF 515 / p.504). It is one author's paper in a separate translation, not Siff and Verkhoshansky. (2) **Missing dedup link.** 6d's `heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block` (PDF 382-383) covers the same strength-then-technique question from the 6.12.2 passage. This entry's angle is different and keeps its place: the emergence-period volume rule, competition-period strength work, and SPP's dominant role. The two entries must link each other. **Contested: upheld.** I checked the image of PDF 536. It says "volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume". That is the reverse of PDF 375 ("easy and painless ... to change to *intensive* loading, but it will react negatively to *extensive* work", italics in the original). The Addendum's own triple-jumper example (a volume rise "by only a few percent" led to "a fast decrease") sides with Ch 6. The entry records both pages and labels the translation-slip idea as Inference, which is right under the brief. | (1) Replace "The Addendum restates" with "Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, translated by Yessis; PDF p. 515) restates". Replace "The authors' own, from the Addendum" with "Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum". Add to the Inference: "the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible". Optional: the Addendum example names "the athlete" (singular) losing national-team selection, so "triple jumpers ... lost both" could read "the athlete lost both". (2) Add `[[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]` to Related, and suggest the reciprocal link to the 6d fixer. Checked: PDF 375-376 quotes; "dominant role" at PDF 376; baseline lines 105 and 186. |
| claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training | FIX | **Unlabelled gloss on Susman.** The entry says: "The authors cite this as evidence that load-induced homeostatic disturbance shows in psycho-physiological indicators, not as a documented LDTE." The source (PDF 377 / p.366) puts Susman 1978 directly after "disturbance of homeostasis can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators". It then describes the indicators rising "as the supercompensation (adaptive reconstruction) phase emerged" after loads were cut. The authors never say "not as a documented LDTE". That framing is the writer's reading. | Reword to: "The authors do not call this an LDTE; they give it after stating that disturbance of homeostasis 'can be detected in the dynamics of a number of psycho-physiological indicators' (PDF p. 377). Inference: it is offered as a sea-level example of the dip-and-rebound pattern in non-aerobic measures, not as a documented LDTE in aerobic productivity." Checked against the PDF 376 image: 1700 m, 3 weeks, more than 4 weeks, peak about 1 week, 2250 m, 4-minute ergometer test, the hypobaric explanation and the "no experimental data" sentence. Title scope is correct. |
| claim--concentrated-beats-distributed-loading-for-highly-qualified-athletes | FIX | (1) **Missing dedup links.** 6b's `framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation` (6.8.1, Fig 6.23) is the passage PDF 371 points back to ("see 6.6.1 and Fig 6.23"). 6d's `claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes` (PDF 379-381) makes the same qualification split for complex vs concentrated loading. This entry has a real new angle (the qualification split, with Kornelyuk's glycolytic data) but links neither. (2) **Italics scope is overstated.** The entry calls the whole conclusion "italicised in the original". On PDF 371 only "concentration of the volume of uni-directional loading produces more extensive functional changes and greater improvement" is italic; "in the athlete's physical fitness" is roman. **Contested: upheld.** The vault Issurin 2016 brief (lines 46-51) is paraphrased accurately. It targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model (line 51), finds the evidence insufficient for broad use in combat, team-sport and swimming preparation, and places the model with narrow-quality sports. This is a disagreement about how far the evidence reaches, not a flat opposite. The Kornelyuk sprinter and jumper evidence sits outside Issurin's named domains; only the boxing study (Filimonov) is inside them, which the entry already notes as Inference. | (1) Add `[[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]]` and `[[claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes]]` to Related. (2) Change to "Their conclusion, partly italicised in the original:". Optional: add to the contested note "Inference: this is a disagreement about scope and evidence sufficiency; the sprinter and jumper studies fall outside the sports Issurin names." Checked: the distributed and concentrated definitions, "both methods are successful", Kornelyuk 1980, Levchenko 1986, Sirenko & Zhdanovich 1982, Filimonov 1979, Mironenko & Antonova 1981, all at PDF 371 / p.360; baseline lines 106, 117, 182. |
| heuristic--within-session-order-of-explosive-means-matters-less-than-volume-and-contrast | FIX | **The contested reason uses a mis-scoped locator and misses the sharpest contradiction.** (1) The entry lists the PDF 301 bullets ("Strength exercises should be done after speed-strength exercises in training"; "Strong-acting plyometric methods should be done after strength exercises") as Chapter 5's fixed orders, set against a within-session rule. On the images of PDF 300-301, those bullets sit under "**The following principles for the sequential use of training means over a given period emerge:**" (PDF 300 / p.289). They are stage-level rules, not session rules. 8. **Nedobyvailov:** Fig 6.25 power GP3 about 20, GP2 about 14; absolute GP2 about 18; speed GP1 about 18.
9. **restoration heuristic:** label two glosses as Inference; add the blank line before Example.

**Verdict: GO AFTER FIXES. 10 GO, 9 FIX, 0 NO-GO.** No entry is wrong at its core. The nine fixes are mostly misread graph values, wrong page references, missing labels and missing links.

**Your special-attention points:**
- **LDTE entries:** They agree with the existing library entries (1-3 week lag at PDF 305, 4-12 weeks as how long the effect lasts at PDF 375) and add new angles: the volume optimum, and the difference between maintaining an effect and the LDTE. No number is restated differently.
- **The three `contested` tags all hold:**
  - **Intensive vs extensive work (PDF 375 vs 536):** the Addendum image really does say the reverse. Its own example agrees with Chapter 6, though, so a translation slip is plausible.
  - **Within-session order:** the conflict is real but sits elsewhere than the entry says. The PDF 301 bullets are rules for sequencing stages, not sessions. The real same-session rule is on PDF 300, which the entry missed. PDF 371 on its own is a hedge, not a contradiction.
  - **Concentrated vs distributed:** the Issurin 2016 brief is stated accurately and does target Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model. It is a disagreement about how far the evidence reaches, not a flat opposite.
- **Figures:** Figs 6.24 and 6.29 read correctly, and the Fig 6.24 units problem is described correctly. Fig 6.30's loading-block start and end are misread, and three Fig 6.25 values are slightly off (fixes 1 and 8). Fig 6.28 has no numbers and no in-scope entry cites it.
- **Same-study link (Fig 6.24 and the Chapter 5 novice experiment):** properly labelled Inference and not asserted.

**Also checked:** every "Eric's baseline:" quote, line number and tag matches `method-baseline.md`. Every link resolves today, including the five into 6a/6b.

**Required fixes:**
1. **LDTE principle:** the Fig 6.30 loading block runs from about month 1.6 to 4.5, not 1.3 to 4.3. Record all three "4-12 weeks" uses: PDF 305, PDF 375, and PDF 536, where the Addendum uses it for stage length. The book's own rule that the effect lasts about as long as the loading stage reconciles 375 and 536.
2. **Technique heuristic:** the Addendum is Verkhoshansky's own paper translated by Yessis (PDF 515), so it should not say "the authors". Add a link to the 6d `heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block`.
3. **Altitude claim:** the Susman 1978 sentence ("not as a documented LDTE") is the writer's reading. Reword it and label it Inference.
4. **Concentrated claim:** add links to the 6b `framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation` and the 6d `claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes`. Only part of the quoted conclusion is italic in the original, so say "partly italicised".
5. **Within-session heuristic:** rewrite the contested reason:
   - PDF 301 is a stage-level rule (see the heading on PDF 300).
   - Add the PDF 300 finding that strength followed by speed-strength in the same session is least effective, from novices and average-level athletes.
   - Call PDF 371 a hedge.
6. **Sequential (4-6 week) heuristic:** label two unlabelled statements as Inference ("so the 4-6 weeks is a minimum" and "Bondarchuk agrees"). Add the PDF 300-301 stage-level rule that strength work comes after speed-strength work.
7. **Time-limits claim:** the "Unclear wording" paragraph counts PDF 372 as evidence against the literal PDF 370 sentence. PDF 372 actually agrees with it; only the PDF 373 sequential model conflicts.
8. **Nedobyvailov (Fig 6.25):** power is about 20 (GP3) and about 14 (GP2). Absolute strength GP2 is about 18 and speed GP1 is about 18.
9. **Restoration heuristic:** label two of the writer's judgments as Inference ("removes part of the signal" and the 15% "confounds" claim). Add the missing blank line before Example.

**Missing ideas (3):**
- The warning against using highly stimulating means too early (PDF 368-369, the section with Fig 6.28).
- Special-preparation exercises must exceed competition conditions to keep their training effect for highly qualified athletes (PDF 367). This may already be partly covered by the 4.3.3 entry.
- 6.8.3: general fitness qualities trained separately do not add up to sport-specific fitness (PDF 363). This may already be covered by the Chapter 1.3 specificity entries.

The report also suggests reciprocal links for the 6b and 6d fixers.
